sections.title: The local Euler defect
sections.intro:
Let \(H\) be a real Banach space, with norm \(\|\cdot\|\). All Lipschitz constants \(L\) below are nonnegative. All time integrals are Bochner integrals. For the Langevin application we will take \(H=L^2(P;\mathbb R^d)\); the norms below then measure random variables in mean square. The scalar defect estimate permits a nonnegative real parameter \(d\); its application uses the natural-number dimension, viewed as a real number. Begin with a Lipschitz drift \(g\), a reference curve \(Y\), and its additive noise \(B\). We first derive the error of freezing the drift over one time step directly from the integral equation.

The analytic calculation is conditional on the displayed integral equation and norm bounds. It neither constructs a stationary Langevin diffusion nor proves its score moment. The Gaussian and Brownian noise moments used later are proved separately.

declarations.name: localDefect
declarations.title: Definition of the local defect
declarations.statement:
For \(g:H\to H\), \(Y:\mathbb R\to H\), and \(h\in\mathbb R\), define the drift omitted when Euler freezes \(g\) at the initial point:

\[D_h(g,Y):=\int_0^h\bigl(g(Y_t)-g(Y_0)\bigr)\,dt.\]

steps.prose: Integrate the difference between the evolving drift and its frozen value. This defines the defect itself; the estimates below will be consequences of this definition.
steps.note: Line 27. ∫ t in 0..h, ... is interval-integral notation: integrate the expression after the comma with respect to the real variable t, from 0 to h. The integrand is the vector g (Y t) - g (Y 0): the current drift minus the drift at time zero. Both occurrences of Y are ordinary function evaluations, not subscripts. This is a Bochner integral, which allows vector-valued integrands. The interval notation is oriented: it also has a defined meaning when h is negative; later estimates explicitly assume nonnegative h. Lean defines integrals even without an integrability hypothesis, while the expected linearity and norm theorems require their stated hypotheses. This line only defines the defect; it does not yet establish an estimate or integrability. Read := in the preceding line as an introduction of the expression, not as an equality that needs a separate proof.

declarations.statement_note: Line 26 starts a definition: def localDefect introduces a new mathematical object. (g : H → H) is a function taking a vector and returning a vector; (Y : ℝ → H) is a time-indexed vector; (h : ℝ) is the endpoint time. Arrows in these types mean “function from … to …”. The final : H specifies that the definition returns one vector. The := means “is defined to be”, with the body on line 27. Here we construct data rather than prove a proposition, so no by proof block is needed. Function application is written with spaces: localDefect g Y h passes the three arguments, and g (Y t) first evaluates Y at t, then applies g. The Banach-space structures from line 23 are implicit ambient parameters.

declarations.name: localDefect_eq_integral_sub
declarations.title: Separate the exact and frozen drift
declarations.statement:
If \(t\mapsto g(Y_t)\) is integrable on the interval between \(0\) and \(h\), then

\[D_h(g,Y)=\int_0^h g(Y_t)\,dt-h\,g(Y_0).\]

steps.prose: Expand the definition. Both the actual drift and the constant function \(g(Y_0)\) are integrable, so linearity separates their difference into two integrals.
steps.note:
Line 33. unfold localDefect replaces the defined name localDefect g Y h in the current goal by its body, the integral of the difference. unfold changes how the goal is displayed by expanding an existing definition; it does not introduce a hypothesis. We now need to compare an integral of a difference with a difference of integrals.

Line 34. rw [...] rewrites the goal using the equality named in its square-bracket list. intervalIntegral.integral_sub is a library theorem saying that the integral of a difference is the difference of the integrals, provided both functions are interval integrable. Spaces apply that theorem to its proofs: hInt supplies integrability of the varying drift, and intervalIntegrable_const supplies integrability of the constant function g (Y 0). Lean infers this constant from the goal. The dot in intervalIntegral.integral_sub separates a namespace from a theorem name. After the rewrite, the remaining issue is to evaluate the integral of that constant.

steps.prose: The integral of the constant vector is \((h-0)g(Y_0)=h\,g(Y_0)\), yielding the identity.
steps.note: Line 35. simp only [...] simplifies the goal using just the listed rules, together with Lean’s basic definitional reductions. intervalIntegral.integral_const changes the constant integral into (h - 0) • g (Y 0), and sub_zero changes h - 0 into h. The square brackets here are a list of simplification rules; they do not mean that hInt is a set member or that a new typeclass is required. Once both sides are identical, simplification closes the equality goal. This is why no further exact line is needed. The theorem has now proved an identity from the integrability assumption rather than merely declaring two expressions interchangeable.

declarations.statement_note: Lines 30–32 declare a theorem, so the expression after the last colon is a proposition to prove. The data are the same g, Y, and h as in the definition. hInt is the name of a supplied proof of IntervalIntegrable (fun t ↦ g (Y t)) volume 0 h: the drift function is integrable over this interval with respect to ordinary Lebesgue measure, called volume. The lambda fun t ↦ ... means “the function taking t to …”; it is not itself a proof. The conclusion says that localDefect g Y h equals the integral of the evolving drift minus h • g (Y 0). The dot • multiplies a vector by a real scalar. := by supplies a proof of this proposition through tactics, with the indented lines forming its body.

declarations.name: localDefect_euler_identity
declarations.title: An exact step is Euler minus its defect
declarations.statement:
Assume the preceding drift integrability and the endpoint integral equation

\[Y_h-Y_0=-\int_0^h g(Y_t)\,dt+B_h.\]

Then the exact reference step has the form

\[Y_h=Y_0-h\,g(Y_0)+B_h-D_h(g,Y).\]

steps.prose: Solve the assumed integral equation for \(Y_h\), then replace the defect by the difference between the exact drift integral and its frozen approximation.
steps.note:
Line 43. rw [sub_eq_iff_eq_add] at heq rewrites the hypothesis named heq, because at heq targets that hypothesis rather than the goal. The library rule changes a - b = c into a = c + b. Here it solves the given integral equation for Y h, producing an equality that can replace the left side of the desired conclusion. Rewriting an equivalence is legitimate because it preserves the truth of the proposition.

Line 44. This rw has no at, so it acts on the goal. The first listed equality, heq, substitutes the expression just obtained for Y h. The second is our previous theorem, applied by spaces to g, Y, h, and the integrability proof hInt. It replaces localDefect g Y h with its exact integral-minus-frozen-drift formula. The square brackets give an ordered list of rewrite rules, not a collection of assumptions. After these replacements, both sides contain the same integral, initial value, and noise; only vector algebra remains.

steps.prose: Cancel the two frozen-drift terms. The resulting equality is precisely the Euler update with the signed remainder \(-D_h\).
steps.note: Line 45. module is a tactic for algebraic identities in modules, such as real vector spaces. It normalizes sums, differences, negation, and scalar multiples and checks that the coefficients of each vector agree. Here it cancels the frozen drift terms h • g (Y 0) with opposite signs and rearranges the remaining vectors. A general vector is not a real number, so the scalar tactic ring would not by itself express the needed module reasoning. This line finishes the entire equality goal; module is a tactic name, not a new hypothesis or a mathematical object. The sign of the remainder is consequently checked: the exact step is Euler minus the defect as defined.

declarations.statement_note: Lines 39–42 take g : H → H, two curves (Y B : ℝ → H), and a real time h. A grouped binder (Y B : ℝ → H) gives both names the same type. hInt again supplies drift integrability. heq is the supplied endpoint integral equation, a proof that Y h - Y 0 equals the negative drift integral plus the noise vector B h. The conclusion rearranges this equation into the Euler update minus localDefect g Y h. Every = in this statement is a proposition; := by begins the proof of the final equality. heq is not a function to calculate a trajectory; it is a named proof available in the local context. The result is conditional on that proof, and makes no existence assertion for the curve.

declarations.name: localDefect_integrable
declarations.title: Continuity supplies drift integrability
declarations.statement: Let \(H\) be a normed additive group, \(g:H\to H\) be \(L\)-Lipschitz with \(L\ge0\), and \(Y:\mathbb R\to H\) be continuous. For every real \(h\), the function \(t\mapsto g(Y_t)\) is interval integrable from \(0\) to \(h\).

steps.prose: A Lipschitz map is continuous, so \(g\circ Y\) is continuous. A continuous function is integrable on every compact interval, proving the claim.
steps.note: Line 53. Read the chained dot notation from left to right. hLip.continuous extracts a proof that a Lipschitz map g is continuous. .comp hY combines it with continuity of Y, giving continuity of the function t ↦ g (Y t). The parentheses collect this whole proof so that .intervalIntegrable 0 h can use it as the input to the library theorem: a continuous function is integrable on the compact interval with endpoints 0 and h. The 0 and h are endpoint arguments, not a range of proof lines. Dot notation here calls theorems with the proof before the dot as an argument; it does not evaluate a numerical attribute. The resulting expression has exactly the proposition required after the theorem’s colon, so it completes the proof without exact, have, or by.

declarations.statement_note: The omit on line 47 records that this theorem does not require the real normed-space or completeness instances. Line 50 has implicit parameters {L : ℝ≥0} and {g : H → H}: Lean can normally recover these from the explicit proof hLip : LipschitzWith L g. The type ℝ≥0 packages a real number with evidence that it is nonnegative. LipschitzWith L g means distances between output vectors are at most L times distances between the inputs. The explicit arguments Y, hY : Continuous Y, and h specify a continuous reference curve and any real interval endpoint. The conclusion is interval integrability of the composite drift. After :=, line 53 supplies a proof term directly rather than opening a by tactic block.

declarations.name: integral_sqrt_zero
declarations.title: The square-root integral
declarations.statement:
For every \(h\ge0\),

\[\int_0^h\sqrt t\,dt=\frac23h\sqrt h.\]

steps.prose: Write \(\sqrt t=t^{1/2}\) and use the power-integral formula. The exponent satisfies \(1/2>-1\), so the formula applies at the zero endpoint.
steps.note:
Line 58. simp_rw [Real.sqrt_eq_rpow] repeatedly rewrites square roots as powers with real exponent 1 / 2. Unlike a single outer rewrite, simp_rw can perform the replacement inside the function under the integral binder. Its square brackets list the rewrite rule. The goal becomes an equality about real powers, which matches the library integral formula.

Line 59. rw [integral_rpow (...)] applies that formula. Its condition is a disjunction; Or.inl chooses the first alternative by providing a proof that the exponent is greater than -1. The parenthesized expression (by norm_num : (-1 : ℝ) < 1 / 2) is a small proof of that numerical inequality. by starts its tactic block, norm_num checks the rational arithmetic, and the following : ... specifies the proposition it proves. This is a proof used as an argument, not a new axiom. Rewriting now produces endpoint powers divided by the exponent plus one.

steps.prose: The contribution at zero vanishes. Since \(h\ge0\), the other endpoint is \(h^{1/2+1}=h^{1/2}h=\sqrt h\,h\).
steps.note:
Line 60. The rw [ list continues onto line 61; the newline does not end the command. Real.zero_rpow evaluates the lower endpoint power at zero. Its argument is a proof that (1 / 2 : ℝ) + 1 ≠ 0, again checked by norm_num. The symbol ≠ means “is not equal to”; this excludes the exceptional exponent. sub_zero then removes the subtraction of that zero endpoint value.

Line 61. Real.rpow_add_one' hh ... rewrites the upper endpoint power into the product of a half-power and h. The trailing apostrophe is part of the theorem’s name, indicating a particular library variant. hh proves the base h is nonnegative, and the second small proof supplies the nonzero exponent condition. The closing ] ends the same rewrite list begun on line 60. The analytic integral calculation is now finished; the goal contains ordinary scalar products and fractions.

steps.prose: Divide by \(1/2+1=3/2\) and rearrange the factors to obtain \((2/3)h\sqrt h\).
steps.note: Line 62. ring proves the remaining real algebra identity by normalizing polynomial expressions with rational coefficients. At this point the half-power of h can be treated as one scalar expression; no new analytic fact about powers is needed. The tactic moves the coefficient 1 / (1 / 2 + 1) into the form 2 / 3 and rearranges multiplication. Because line 58 also rewrote the square root on the right side, the resulting terms match after normalization. ring is a proof-generating tactic, so Lean still checks its result; it is not a numerical approximation and introduces no rounding error.

declarations.statement_note: Line 56 introduces a real number h and a named hypothesis hh : 0 ≤ h. The final colon introduces the equality to prove. Real.sqrt is the real square-root function, written with its namespace to distinguish it from other operations. (2 / 3 : ℝ) is a type annotation: the fraction is interpreted as a real number, so it is not natural-number division. * is real multiplication, unlike vector scalar multiplication •. The conclusion evaluates the integral explicitly. := by begins a tactic proof; we convert square roots to real powers to use mathlib’s power-integral formula, then convert the endpoint result into the requested shape. No assumption says h is strictly positive, so the proof must also handle h = 0.

declarations.name: integral_equation_increment_bound
declarations.title: Bound a reference increment
declarations.statement:
Let \(h\ge0\) and suppose that, for every \(0\le s\le h\),

\[\|g(Y_s)\|\le G,\qquad \|B_s\|\le N\sqrt s,\qquad Y_s-Y_0=-\int_0^s g(Y_r)\,dr+B_s.\]

Then, for each \(0\le t\le h\),

\[\|Y_t-Y_0\|\le tG+N\sqrt t.\]

steps.prose:
First bound the drift integral on \([0,t]\) by its constant norm bound:

\[\left\|\int_0^t g(Y_s)\,ds\right\|\le G\,|t-0|=Gt,\]

where \(t\ge0\) removes the absolute value.
steps.note:
Line 74. have hdrift : ... := by announces a local intermediate fact called hdrift, specifies its proposition after :, and opens a subproof after := by. This particular fact bounds the drift integral by G * t. Once its indented proof finishes, hdrift becomes available to the rest of the theorem. See what have does.

Line 75. have hb := ... creates another local fact; because no type is written after hb, Lean infers its proposition from the theorem applied on this and the next line. intervalIntegral.norm_integral_le_of_norm_le_const bounds an integral’s norm when its integrand has a constant norm bound.

Line 76. Named arguments (a := 0), (b := t), (C := G), and (f := fun s ↦ g (Y s)) tell Lean exactly which interval, bound, and function to use. Here := fills an argument name; it does not define the global symbol a. The lambda (fun s hs ↦ ?_) supplies a proof for arbitrary s and interval-membership evidence hs; ?_ asks Lean to create a subgoal for the missing proof.

Line 77. The bullet · starts one focused subgoal. simpa [abs_of_nonneg ht.1] using hb simplifies the proposition proved by hb until it matches the announced target for hdrift. ht.1 extracts 0 ≤ t from the pair of inequalities represented by ht. It lets abs_of_nonneg replace |t| by t, while simplification also removes t - 0. simpa therefore uses an existing proof after simplification, rather than asserting a new bound without evidence.

steps.prose: To justify the constant bound under that integral, note that \(s\in(0,t]\) implies \(0\le s\le t\le h\). Hence the assumed bound on \([0,h]\) applies to every such \(s\).
steps.note:
Line 78. This second · addresses the hole ?_ from line 76. hs initially describes membership in the unordered half-open interval Set.uIoc 0 t required by the integral theorem. rw [Set.uIoc_of_le ht.1] at hs uses 0 ≤ t to identify it with Set.Ioc 0 t, so hs.1 is 0 < s and hs.2 is s ≤ t. at hs changes that local hypothesis only.

Line 79. exact closes the goal by supplying a proof with exactly the required type. hG s ... applies the assumed bound at time s; the missing argument is evidence that s ∈ Set.Icc 0 h. The pair ⟨hs.1.le, hs.2.trans ht.2⟩ supplies it: .le weakens 0 < s to 0 ≤ s, and .trans ht.2 combines s ≤ t with t ≤ h. Angle brackets construct the two-part membership proof. The pointwise bound is now established, completing the subproof of hdrift.

steps.prose:
Insert the integral equation and apply the triangle inequality:

\[\|Y_t-Y_0\|\le\left\|\int_0^t g(Y_s)\,ds\right\|+\|B_t\|.\]

Negation leaves the norm of the drift integral unchanged.
steps.note:
Line 80. rw [heq t ht] applies the integral-equation hypothesis at t, using ht as its domain proof, then replaces Y t - Y 0 in the goal by the negative drift integral plus B t.

Line 81. calc begins a chain of equalities or inequalities. Lean checks each step and combines them by transitivity. The first left-hand expression matches the goal after the previous rewrite.

Line 82. This line writes the norm of the sum of the negative integral and the noise, followed by ≤. It begins the first comparison in the chain; the right side continues on line 83. The parentheses ensure that unary minus applies to the whole integral.

Line 83. The right side is the sum of the integral norm and the noise norm. := by introduces the justification for this single comparison. This colon-equals supplies a proof of a calc step, just as it supplies a proof of a theorem.

Line 84. norm_add_le is the triangle inequality, applied to the two vectors displayed in parentheses. Its conclusion initially contains the norm of a negative integral. simpa only [norm_neg] using ... removes that minus sign inside the norm and supplies exactly the comparison written on lines 82–83. only restricts simplification to that named rule.

steps.prose: Apply the two bounds to obtain \(Gt+N\sqrt t\), and commute the factors \(G\) and \(t\).
steps.note:
Line 85. The _ at the start of a later calc line stands for the previous right-hand side; Lean infers it, rather than creating an unfinished proof. add_le_add hdrift (hB t ht) adds two proved inequalities. hdrift bounds the drift integral, and hB t ht is the assumed noise bound at this same time t. Spaces apply the theorem to these proof arguments. This establishes the next bound in the chain, with coefficient G * t.

Line 86. The last step changes G * t to t * G. := by ring supplies a short scalar-algebra proof of that equality. Multiplication of real numbers commutes, and the remaining summand is unchanged. The complete chain now has the original increment norm on the left and exactly the desired expression on the right. Finishing the calc also finishes the theorem’s proof.

declarations.statement_note: Lines 67–73 describe a conditional estimate. g is a vector field; Y and B are curves; h, G, and N are real parameters. _hh : 0 ≤ h is an assumption whose initial underscore signals it is intentionally unused directly in this proof. The hypotheses hG, hB, and heq are universally quantified statements on the closed interval Set.Icc 0 h. ∀ t ∈ Set.Icc 0 h, ... means “for every t, if t belongs to this interval, then …”; using such a hypothesis requires both a time and a membership proof. The implicit {t : ℝ} is the particular time under consideration, while ht proves 0 ≤ t and t ≤ h. The conclusion bounds the increment norm by t * G + N * Real.sqrt t. omit [CompleteSpace H] removes completeness for this theorem.

declarations.name: localDefect_bound
declarations.title: Integrate the Lipschitz increment bound
declarations.statement:
Assume \(h\ge0\), \(g\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz with \(L\ge0\), and for \(0\le t\le h\) the same integral equation and bounds \(\|g(Y_t)\|\le G\), \(\|B_t\|\le N\sqrt t\) hold. Then

\[\|D_h(g,Y)\|\le L\left(\frac{h^2G}{2}+\frac23h\sqrt h\,N\right).\]

steps.prose: For \(0\[\|g(Y_t)-g(Y_0)\|\le L\|Y_t-Y_0\|.\]
steps.note:
Line 100. have hbound (t : ℝ) (ht : t ∈ Set.Ioc 0 h) : begins a locally proved, parameterized fact. It will be usable later as hbound t ht. Here Set.Ioc 0 h is the interval 0 < t ≤ h, whereas the assumptions use the closed interval Set.Icc 0 h.

Line 101. This continuation gives the exact inequality proved by hbound: the norm of the drift difference is bounded by (L : ℝ) * (t * G + N * Real.sqrt t). The final := by starts its subproof; t and ht are available only within this parameterized local argument.

Line 102. calc organizes that subproof as two inequalities, first using Lipschitz continuity, then the increment bound.

Line 103. The first inequality replaces the drift difference by L times the state difference. Its := by introduces a proof just for this step.

Line 104. hLip.dist_le_mul (Y t) (Y 0) is the Lipschitz distance estimate at these two vectors. simpa only [dist_eq_norm] using ... rewrites both distances as norms of differences so the library estimate has the displayed form. hLip is the supplied proof, .dist_le_mul is a theorem accessed through dot notation, and the two parenthesized expressions are its input points.

steps.prose:
Multiply the increment estimate by \(L\ge0\) to obtain the pointwise majorant

\[\|g(Y_t)-g(Y_0)\|\le L(tG+N\sqrt t).\]
steps.note:
Line 105. The _ inherits the previous right-hand expression, L * ‖Y t - Y 0‖. The new right side is the desired pointwise majorant, leaving only the replacement of the increment norm to justify. The := makes the following expression the proof of this comparison.

Line 106. mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_left says an inequality may be multiplied on the left by a nonnegative scalar. It needs the underlying inequality and a proof of nonnegativity, supplied on the next two lines.

Line 107. The earlier theorem integral_equation_increment_bound is applied to g Y B h G N hh hG hB heq in order. The final argument ⟨ht.1.le, ht.2⟩ turns the open-left interval membership into the closed-interval membership that theorem requires. Here ht.1 is 0 < t; .le weakens it to 0 ≤ t.

Line 108. L.coe_nonneg is evidence that the real value of L : ℝ≥0 is nonnegative. It fills the sign condition for line 106. The resulting proof finishes hbound; the main theorem can now use that named function to obtain a bound at each allowed time.

steps.prose: The scalar majorant \(t\mapsto L(tG+N\sqrt t)\) is continuous, hence integrable on \([0,h]\).
steps.note:
Line 109. have hbint : IntervalIntegrable begins another named fact, this time establishing integrability of the scalar majorant. It is a proposition, not a new numerical integral value.

Line 110. The function is written explicitly as fun t : ℝ ↦ ...; the annotation fixes the lambda input type. volume 0 h specifies Lebesgue measure and the two interval endpoints. The := means the next expression must prove this whole integrability proposition.

Line 111. (by fun_prop : Continuous ... ) is a typed proof term. fun_prop uses registered continuity facts for constants, addition, multiplication, and real square root. The proposition being proved starts with Continuous and continues on line 112.

Line 112. The closing parenthesis ends that continuity proof. .intervalIntegrable _ _ turns it into interval integrability. Each _ is an inference placeholder: Lean recovers the endpoints 0 and h from the declared type of hbint. These underscores do not leave unproved goals, unlike an unresolved ?_. This establishes the integrability condition needed to integrate the majorant.

steps.prose:
Expand \(D_h\). The norm estimate for a Bochner integral, together with the integrable majorant, gives

\[\|D_h\|\le\int_0^h L(tG+N\sqrt t)\,dt.\]
steps.note:
Line 113. unfold localDefect expands the left side of the goal into the defining interval integral. It changes the goal’s expression, not the hypotheses.

Line 114. calc now starts the main chain: first compare the integral’s norm with an integral of the scalar bound, then evaluate that bound.

Line 115. This line begins the norm comparison with the actual vector integrand. g (Y t) - g (Y 0) is exactly the difference bounded by hbound.

Line 116. The comparison’s right side integrates the scalar majorant. The := at the end says that lines 117–118 provide a proof term for this inequality.

Line 117. intervalIntegral.norm_integral_le_of_norm_le hh is the norm estimate for an interval Bochner integral with a majorant. hh establishes the order 0 ≤ h of the endpoints. Its other arguments follow on line 118.

Line 118. Filter.Eventually.of_forall hbound packages our bound at every allowed time as the almost-everywhere bound required by the integral theorem. An everywhere statement implies an almost-everywhere statement. The final hbint supplies integrability of the majorant. Applying a theorem to all these proof arguments yields the displayed inequality; no measurability or sign condition is being silently guessed.

steps.prose:
Pull out constants and split the two integrable summands. Evaluate

\[\int_0^h t\,dt=\frac{h^2}{2},\qquad \int_0^h\sqrt t\,dt=\frac23h\sqrt h.\]

This leaves the two drift and noise contributions in the claimed expression.
steps.note:
Line 119. The _ is the integral of the scalar majorant from the previous step. This calc equality states its exact value. := by starts the proof by linearity and the two elementary integrals.

Line 120. rw [intervalIntegral.integral_const_mul, ...] begins one rewrite list lasting through line 125. The first rule pulls the fixed real scalar L outside the integral.

Line 121. intervalIntegral.integral_add splits the integral of t * G + N * Real.sqrt t into two integrals. That equality requires both summands to be integrable; the next two lines supply those arguments directly.

Line 122. (by fun_prop : Continuous (fun t : ℝ ↦ t * G)).intervalIntegrable 0 h proves that the first summand is continuous and then interval integrable. The parentheses delimit the continuity proof before dot notation calls the integrability theorem.

Line 123. The same construction proves integrability of fun t : ℝ ↦ N * Real.sqrt t. The closing parenthesis ends the second argument of integral_add; the comma resumes the rewrite list.

Line 124. intervalIntegral.integral_mul_const pulls a constant on the right of a product outside an integral, and intervalIntegral.integral_const_mul does so for a constant on the left. Their differing names reflect the order of the factors in the integrands.

Line 125. integral_id evaluates the integral of the identity function t ↦ t. integral_sqrt_zero h hh evaluates the square-root integral using our earlier theorem and the nonnegative-time hypothesis. The closing ] ends the list. We are left with scalar expressions that differ only by the order and grouping of products and fractions.

steps.prose: Rearrange the scalar factors to place the drift term first and the noise term second.
steps.note: Line 126. ring proves the remaining scalar equality exactly, rearranging real factors and rational coefficients into the form announced on line 119. It treats Real.sqrt h as a scalar expression and does not need to evaluate it numerically. The result completes the equality in the calc chain, and thus the theorem. The reason the coefficient 2 / 3 appears is the square-root integral proved above; ring only arranges that coefficient after the integral has already been evaluated.

declarations.statement_note: Lines 92–99 take g, the curves Y and B, a nonnegative Lipschitz constant L : ℝ≥0, and real constants h, G, N. (L : ℝ) explicitly views the nonnegative-real object as an ordinary real number so it can appear in scalar arithmetic. The named proofs hh, hLip, hG, hB, and heq respectively give nonnegative time, the Lipschitz property, the two norm bounds on Set.Icc 0 h, and the integral equation there. Each ∀ t ∈ ... hypothesis takes both a time and a membership proof. The conclusion bounds ‖localDefect g Y h‖ by a sum of a drift term and a square-root noise term, multiplied by L. Exponent ^ 2 squares a real number; / 2 is real division. omit [CompleteSpace H] records the weaker ambient requirements of this lemma.

declarations.name: dalalyan_constant_bound
declarations.title: The exact rational constant
declarations.statement:
The numerical factor in the corrected Dalalyan–Karagulyan estimate satisfies

\[\frac76\sqrt2\le\frac{33}{20}=1.65.\]

steps.prose: Use \((\sqrt2)^2=2\) and \(\sqrt2\ge0\). Comparing squares proves the bound, since \(49/18\le1089/400\).
steps.note:
Line 130. have hs := Real.sq_sqrt (...) names a proved equality hs; Lean infers its type because the line omits an explicit : proposition. Real.sq_sqrt states that the square of the square root of a nonnegative real is the original real. Its input proof (by norm_num : (0 : ℝ) ≤ 2) checks the required nonnegativity. Thus hs says (Real.sqrt 2) ^ 2 = 2.

Line 131. have hp := Real.sqrt_nonneg (2 : ℝ) names a proof hp that 0 ≤ Real.sqrt 2. The annotation ensures the literal 2 is real. These named hypotheses give both the magnitude and sign information needed to compare expressions involving the square root.

Line 132. nlinarith is nonlinear arithmetic automation. It combines polynomial equalities and inequalities from the local context, including hs and hp, to derive the target bound. It can treat Real.sqrt 2 as an unknown real constrained by those facts, so it does not rely on a floating-point decimal for the square root. Lean checks the resulting arithmetic proof. This is why the final 33 / 20 bound is an exact rational inequality.

declarations.statement_note: Line 129 is a theorem with no explicit parameters: its proposition is the concrete real inequality (7 / 6 : ℝ) * Real.sqrt 2 ≤ 33 / 20. The annotation : ℝ on the first fraction fixes the surrounding arithmetic as real arithmetic. The right fraction is exact, not a decimal approximation. := by opens a proof. The two have commands below supply facts about Real.sqrt 2; a nonlinear arithmetic tactic can then verify the comparison using its sign and square. This is a small independent numerical lemma that later replaces a square-root coefficient with the convenient rational constant 33 / 20.

declarations.name: localDefect_dalalyan_bound
declarations.title: The local error with stationary moment scales
declarations.statement:
Let \(h,d\in\mathbb R\) with \(h,d\ge0\), let \(g\) be \(L\)-Lipschitz with \(L\ge0\), and suppose \(Lh\le2\). Assume that, for every \(0\le t\le h\),

\[Y_t-Y_0=-\int_0^t g(Y_s)\,ds+B_t,\quad \|g(Y_t)\|\le\sqrt{Ld},\quad \|B_t\|\le\sqrt{2d}\sqrt t.\]

Then

\[\boxed{\|D_h(g,Y)\|\le\frac{33}{20}Lh\sqrt{hd}.}\]

In \(L^2\), the drift bound corresponds to a score second moment at most \(Ld\); here that bound remains a hypothesis.

steps.prose: Compare the nonnegative quantities \(h\sqrt{Ld}\) and \(\sqrt2\sqrt{hd}\) by squaring. It suffices to show \(h^2Ld\le2hd\).
steps.note:
Line 145. have hsmall : ... announces an auxiliary scalar comparison. The first side is h * Real.sqrt ((L : ℝ) * d); it will control the drift contribution in the final estimate.

Line 146. This continuation supplies the comparison’s other side, Real.sqrt 2 * Real.sqrt (h * d), and := by opens its proof. The name hsmall will later refer to a proof of this inequality, not to the step size itself.

Line 147. sq_le_sq₀ is an equivalence between an inequality of squares and the corresponding inequality of nonnegative real numbers. The two (by positivity) arguments prove that the two unsquared expressions are nonnegative, using hh, hd, and the nonnegativity of square roots. .mp selects the direction from the squared inequality to the unsquared one. apply uses that implication backwards: the new goal is now the squared comparison, whose proof will establish hsmall.

steps.prose:
Replace each squared square root by its nonnegative argument. Multiply \(Lh\le2\) by \(hd\ge0\), obtaining \(h^2Ld\le2hd\), and thus

\[h\sqrt{Ld}\le\sqrt2\sqrt{hd}.\]
steps.note:
Line 148. rw [mul_pow, mul_pow, ...] expands squares of products on both sides. Real.sq_sqrt (mul_nonneg L.coe_nonneg hd) replaces the square of sqrt (L * d) by L * d; its proof argument establishes the product is nonnegative.

Line 149. The same list evaluates the squares of sqrt 2 and sqrt (h * d). The first uses a numerical proof from norm_num, and the second uses mul_nonneg hh hd. The brackets close the rewrite list. We now have a polynomial inequality without these squared square-root expressions.

Line 150. have hb := mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_right hstep (mul_nonneg hh hd) names the step-size inequality multiplied by the nonnegative quantity h * d. The theorem takes the original inequality hstep and the sign proof for the multiplier. Its conclusion is a bound on (L * h) * (h * d) by 2 * (h * d).

Line 151. nlinarith rearranges this polynomial consequence to solve the squared goal. When that subproof finishes, the original unsquared inequality is available as hsmall. The squaring step was justified by explicit nonnegativity, so no extraneous negative solution was introduced.

steps.prose:
Split products under the square roots and rearrange:

\[h\sqrt h\sqrt{2d}=h\sqrt2\sqrt{hd}.\]

The nonnegativity of \(h\) and \(2\) justifies the square-root product identities.
steps.note:
Line 152. have hnoise : ... introduces an exact equality for the noise factor. It is an equality, unlike the inequality proved as hsmall; the two different proof types matter when these facts are later used.

Line 153. This continuation gives the desired regrouped form h * Real.sqrt 2 * Real.sqrt (h * d) and opens the subproof with := by. The common factor h stays outside the square roots.

Line 154. rw [Real.sqrt_mul ..., Real.sqrt_mul hh] rewrites square roots of products as products of square roots. The first sign condition is 0 ≤ 2, checked by norm_num; the second is hh : 0 ≤ h. The theorem’s sign conditions are necessary because the real square-root identity is stated for the appropriate nonnegative factor. Square brackets list the two rewrites in order.

Line 155. ring rearranges the now-expanded products to prove the equality. It needs no further facts about square roots because the same factors appear on both sides. The result is stored as hnoise for use in the main comparison chain.

steps.prose:
Apply the two-term local-defect bound with \(G=\sqrt{Ld}\) and \(N=\sqrt{2d}\):

\[\|D_h\|\le L\left(\frac{h^2\sqrt{Ld}}2+\frac23h\sqrt h\sqrt{2d}\right).\]
steps.note:
Line 156. calc starts the final comparison of the defect norm with the target numerical expression. Each later _ will inherit the preceding right side.

Line 157. The first comparison applies the general two-term defect bound; this line begins its right side with the common real Lipschitz factor (L : ℝ).

Line 158. The first term substitutes the drift scale Real.sqrt ((L : ℝ) * d) for the generic bound G. The outer parentheses continue through the next line.

Line 159. The second term substitutes the noise scale Real.sqrt (2 * d) for N. The final := introduces a proof term for the whole inequality on lines 157–159.

Line 160. localDefect_bound g Y B L h (Real.sqrt ((L : ℝ) * d)) applies our general theorem to the same data and the chosen drift bound. Spaces supply positional arguments, with parentheses grouping the square-root expression into one argument.

Line 161. The first expression is the chosen noise bound; hh hLip hG hB heq then provide exactly the required hypotheses. Line wrapping does not change the order of arguments. The theorem application proves the first comparison in calc.

steps.prose:
Bound the first term using \(h\sqrt{Ld}\le\sqrt2\sqrt{hd}\), and rewrite the second with the preceding identity. Since \(1/2+2/3=7/6\),

\[\|D_h\|\le L\frac76\sqrt2\,h\sqrt{hd}.\]
steps.note:
Line 162. This comparison aims to replace the sum of two terms by the combined factor 7 / 6. := by opens a subproof for this inequality only; the rest of the calc follows afterwards.

Line 163. have hb := mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_left hsmall (mul_nonneg hh L.coe_nonneg) multiplies hsmall on the left by the nonnegative scalar h * L. The resulting inequality controls the first, quadratic-in-h, drift term after rearrangement. Lean checks the sign using the two supplied proofs.

Line 164. Inside the rewrite list, show ... by ring constructs an equality on the spot. It begins regrouping the noise product to make the exact left side of hnoise appear as one parenthesized factor.

Line 165. This continuation completes that equality; by ring proves it by scalar algebra. The second rewrite rule, hnoise, then replaces the grouped product using our named identity. show here specifies a proposition that the inline proof must establish; it does not introduce a new assumption.

Line 166. nlinarith combines the bound hb with the rewritten noise term and exact rational arithmetic, including 1 / 2 + 2 / 3 = 7 / 6, to finish this comparison. This produces the intermediate square-root coefficient needed for the final numerical lemma.

steps.prose: Multiply \((7/6)\sqrt2\le33/20\) by the nonnegative factor \(Lh\sqrt{hd}\). This gives the claimed constant without numerical rounding.
steps.note:
Line 167. The last calc comparison has exactly the theorem’s required right side, (33 / 20 : ℝ) * L * h * sqrt (h * d). Its proof starts after := by.

Line 168. have hb := mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_right dalalyan_constant_bound ... uses the already proved numerical inequality (7 / 6) * sqrt 2 ≤ 33 / 20 and multiplies it by a common nonnegative factor supplied on line 169.

Line 169. show 0 ≤ (L : ℝ) * h * Real.sqrt (h * d) by positivity explicitly states that sign goal and proves it from nonnegative factors. It is passed as the second argument to the multiplication theorem. The word show clarifies which proposition the short positivity proof is solving.

Line 170. nlinarith rearranges the products in hb into the order used in the calc line. The exact coefficient 33 / 20 is therefore justified by a checked inequality, and all previous comparisons combine to prove the final bound. The theorem finishes here; neither a numerical approximation nor an additional probabilistic assumption is inserted by this tactic.

declarations.statement_note: Lines 137–144 specialize the preceding defect estimate. The vector field g, curves Y and B, and Lipschitz constant L : ℝ≥0 retain their earlier meanings. Here both h and d are real parameters; hh and hd say they are nonnegative, and hstep is the step-size restriction (L : ℝ) * h ≤ 2. The hypothesis hG gives the drift scale sqrt (L * d) and hB gives the noise scale sqrt (2 * d) * sqrt t, at all times in the closed interval. heq supplies the same integral equation. The conclusion is a single explicit bound for the defined defect. It remains conditional on these moment-scale hypotheses: the theorem does not establish stationarity or derive the score moment. The proof first bounds two scalar expressions, then inserts them into the general defect bound.

sections.setup_note:
Lines 1–4 import existing mathlib results about elementary integrals, interval integrals, Lipschitz maps, and tactics. An import makes definitions and proved theorems available; it does not assume the result currently being proved. Lines 6–14 are a documentation comment, enclosed by /-! and -/, with no effect on the proof. Line 16, noncomputable section, permits definitions using mathematical constructions for which Lean need not produce executable numerical code, such as Bochner integration. Line 18, open MeasureTheory, lets us write IntervalIntegrable instead of its full namespace-qualified name. Line 19, open scoped NNReal, enables scoped notation such as ℝ≥0. Line 21 puts subsequent declarations in namespace ULA, so their full names begin ULA..

Line 23 declares the common ambient setting. {H : Type*} says that H is a type of mathematical objects; braces make this an implicit parameter that Lean normally infers. [NormedAddCommGroup H] supplies addition, subtraction, a norm, and their laws. [NormedSpace ℝ H] supplies real scalar multiplication, written •; [CompleteSpace H] says Cauchy sequences converge. These square brackets request typeclass instances, which Lean searches for automatically; they are different from a rewriting list such as rw [sub_zero]. Together these structures make H a real Banach space. A declaration beginning omit ... in temporarily removes the named ambient instance requirement for the next declaration, recording that its proof needs fewer assumptions. See types and values and the three kinds of binders.

sections.title: Gaussian and Brownian noise moments
sections.intro:
Fix a natural-number dimension \(d\in\mathbb N\), write \(E_d=\mathbb R^d\) with its Euclidean norm, and let \(P\) be a measure on \(\Omega\). A law statement \(X_i\sim\mathcal N(0,v)\) below means that the coordinate is almost everywhere measurable and has the stated pushforward measure. We prove the required \(L^2\) norms from these laws. Coordinate independence is unnecessary for second moments because \(\|X\|^2=\sum_iX_i^2\) has no cross terms.

For Brownian processes the input is mathlib’s actual scalar pre-Brownian law predicate, whose marginal and increment laws supply the Gaussian hypotheses. These facts establish the noise moments; existence and stationarity of a coupled Langevin reference require separate inputs.

declarations.name: centered_gaussian_second_moment
declarations.title: Second moment of a centered Gaussian
declarations.statement:
For nonnegative variance \(v\), the centered Gaussian law has second moment

\[\int_{\mathbb R}x^2\,d\mathcal N(0,v)(x)=v.\]

steps.prose: The known Gaussian variance is \(v\). Expand variance as \(\int(x-\mathbb E[x])^2\), and insert the Gaussian mean \(\mathbb E[x]=0\).
steps.note:
Line 27. have hv := ... creates a local fact named hv; Lean infers its proposition from the theorem on the right. variance_fun_id_gaussianReal gives the variance of the identity random variable under a Gaussian measure. (μ := 0) and (v := v) are named arguments: the first v in (v := v) is the library parameter name and the second is our local variance value. This use of := fills argument slots; it does not assign a new value to our local parameter. The fact hv initially expresses variance, which is not yet written as the desired second-moment integral.

Line 28. rw [...] at hv rewrites that local fact rather than the goal. variance_eq_integral expands variance as the integral of the squared deviation from the mean. Its proof argument measurable_id'.aemeasurable supplies the almost-everywhere measurability of the identity function; the apostrophe is part of the theorem name. integral_id_gaussianReal then evaluates the Gaussian mean, which is zero in this case. The square brackets contain an ordered list of two rewrite rules. The resulting hv is the desired moment equality except for subtractions of zero inside the square.

steps.prose: Simplify \(x-0=x\). The variance integral is now exactly the required second moment.
steps.note: Line 29. simpa only [sub_zero] using hv closes the goal with the existing proof hv after simplifying its proposition. sub_zero replaces every relevant x - 0 by x; only restricts the explicitly used simplification rules. The word using identifies the proof to simplify and reuse. This differs from simp alone, which tries to close the current goal by simplification without naming such a source proof. After the change, hv proves the integral of x ^ 2 equals (v : ℝ), exactly as required. No new Gaussian theorem is being assumed here; this finishes the reduction of the library variance theorem to the centered second moment.

declarations.statement_note: Line 25 introduces the nonnegative variance parameter (v : ℝ≥0). The theorem’s conclusion on line 26 is an equality of real numbers. gaussianReal 0 v is the real Gaussian measure with mean zero and variance v; the variance is nonnegative by its type. ∫ x : ℝ, x ^ 2 ∂gaussianReal 0 v means the integral of the function x ↦ x² against this specific measure. The symbol ∂ introduces the integration measure; it is not a derivative here. (v : ℝ) coerces the nonnegative-real parameter to an ordinary real number so that it has the same type as the integral. The proof starts with the library’s variance identity, then removes the centered mean. Zero variance is allowed.

declarations.name: gaussian_vector_memLp
declarations.title: Gaussian coordinates give a square-integrable vector
declarations.statement: Let \(X:\Omega\to E_d\), and suppose every coordinate satisfies \(X_i\sim\mathcal N(0,v)\) under \(P\), with \(v\ge0\). Then \(X\in L^2(P;E_d)\).

steps.prose: In finite-dimensional Euclidean space, square integrability is equivalent to square integrability of each coordinate. Each coordinate belongs to \(L^2\) because its Gaussian law has a finite second moment; transfer that membership along the equality of laws.
steps.note:
Line 35. memLp_piLp_iff is a library equivalence saying that a function with values in a finite-coordinate PiLp space is square integrable exactly when each coordinate function is square integrable. .mpr selects the implication from coordinate membership to vector membership. apply works backwards with that implication: the goal MemLp X 2 P becomes “every coordinate has MemLp”. The dot here selects a direction of an equivalence, not a field of the vector X.

Line 36. intro i proves the universal statement by fixing an arbitrary index i : Fin d. The new goal is square integrability of the scalar function fun ω ↦ X ω i. Because i is arbitrary, a proof under this local name will establish the required statement for every coordinate, including the vacuous case when the index type is empty.

Line 37. hlaw i is the supplied Gaussian-law proof for this coordinate. Its .memLp theorem transports Lp membership from the law measure back to the original sample space. memLp_id_gaussianReal (2 : ℝ≥0) supplies the Gaussian identity variable’s finite second moment; the annotation fixes the exponent argument as a nonnegative real. exact supplies the transported proof to close the coordinate goal and hence the original vector goal.

declarations.statement_note: Lines 32–34 take an ordinary random-vector function X : Ω → E d and a nonnegative variance v. The hypothesis hlaw : ∀ i : Fin d, HasLaw (fun ω ↦ X ω i) (gaussianReal 0 v) P is a function assigning a proof of the stated Gaussian law to each coordinate index i. fun ω ↦ X ω i holds i fixed and extracts a scalar random variable from the vector. HasLaw includes almost-everywhere measurability and equality of the pushforward measure with this Gaussian measure. The conclusion MemLp X 2 P is a proposition: X is almost-everywhere strongly measurable and has finite L² seminorm. The exponent 2 specifies square integrability. This is not yet an element of the quotient space Lp (E d) 2 P; construction of that class comes later via .toLp X.

declarations.name: gaussian_vector_second_moment
declarations.title: Sum the coordinate moments
declarations.statement:
Under the same coordinate Gaussian laws,

\[\int_\Omega\|X(\omega)\|^2\,dP(\omega)=dv.\]

steps.prose: For each coordinate \(i\), retain the proved square integrability \(X_i\in L^2(P)\). It will justify integrating the finite sum of squared coordinates.
steps.note:
Line 43. have hmem (i : Fin d) : MemLp ... := declares a local parameterized proof. Unlike a single proof hmem, this name can later be applied to any coordinate as hmem i. The proposition concerns the scalar coordinate function fun ω ↦ X ω i, exponent 2, and measure P. Its justification continues on line 44.

Line 44. (hlaw i).memLp (...) transports Gaussian identity-variable L² membership to coordinate i, exactly as in the previous theorem. The final parentheses group memLp_id_gaussianReal (2 : ℝ≥0) as the proof argument. This establishes a reusable integrability fact needed before the integral of a finite sum can be split. No new random variable is defined: hmem i is evidence of a property of the already supplied X.

steps.prose:
Change variables using the law of \(X_i\), then apply the scalar Gaussian moment:

\[\int_\Omega X_i^2\,dP=\int_{\mathbb R}x^2\,d\mathcal N(0,v)=v.\]
steps.note:
Line 45. have hmom (i : Fin d) : ... := by introduces another local family of facts: each coordinate’s squared moment equals v. This is now an equality about integrals, whereas hmem was an integrability proposition. The index binder makes the proof reusable for every summand later.

Line 46. (hlaw i).integral_comp transports the integral along the known law, expressing the integral of (X ω i)² as the integral of x² under gaussianReal 0 v. (f := fun x : ℝ ↦ x ^ 2) supplies the test function explicitly by name. (by fun_prop) proves its required almost-everywhere strong measurability using registered function-property rules. The pipe |> passes this equality as the input to .trans, equality transitivity; it is a term-level pipeline, not a tactic separator.

Line 47. centered_gaussian_second_moment v proves the second equality in that transitive chain, from the Gaussian integral to v. The parentheses make this one argument of .trans. exact at the beginning of line 46 therefore supplies the full two-stage proof of hmom i: transport to the Gaussian measure, then evaluate the scalar moment.

steps.prose:
Expand the squared Euclidean norm and interchange the finite sum and integral:

\[\int_\Omega\|X\|^2\,dP=\sum_{i=0}^{d-1}\int_\Omega X_i^2\,dP.\]

Every summand is integrable by its \(L^2\) membership.
steps.note:
Line 48. simp_rw [EuclideanSpace.real_norm_sq_eq] rewrites the squared Euclidean norm inside the integral into a finite sum of squared coordinates. simp_rw works under the integral binder, where a plain rewrite at the outside might not expose all occurrences. The exact formula is a finite sum over Fin d, so no limit or infinite-series interchange is involved.

Line 49. rw [integral_finsetSum _ (fun i _ ↦ (hmem i).integrable_sq)] moves the integral through that finite sum. The theorem requires each summand to be integrable. The lambda fixes a coordinate i and ignores the second input, written _, which is evidence that the coordinate belongs to the finite index set. (hmem i).integrable_sq converts coordinate L² membership into integrability of its square. The earlier standalone _ is an inference placeholder for an argument recoverable from the goal, not an unproved mathematical assertion.

steps.prose: Each of the \(d\) summands equals \(v\); hence their sum is \(dv\).
steps.note: Line 50. simp only [...] now evaluates the sum using the listed exact rules. hmom replaces each coordinate integral by v; Lean supplies its coordinate argument as needed. Finset.sum_const sums a constant over a finite set, Finset.card_univ identifies the size of the full index set, and Fintype.card_fin gives that Fin d has d elements. nsmul_eq_mul rewrites repeated addition of the same real value as multiplication by the natural-number count viewed in the scalar type. This produces (d : ℝ) * (v : ℝ) and closes the equality. The square-bracket list is a collection of simplification lemmas; it does not assert independence or create a distribution.

declarations.statement_note: Lines 40–42 use the same vector X, nonnegative variance v, and coordinate-law proof hlaw. The conclusion integrates ‖X ω‖ ^ 2 with respect to P, then identifies it with (d : ℝ) * (v : ℝ). Both type annotations are coercions: the natural-number dimension and nonnegative-real variance are viewed as real values because the moment is real-valued. ‖X ω‖ is the Euclidean norm of one vector at outcome ω; this is a pointwise norm, not yet the norm of an L² equivalence class. The proof first obtains integrability and the exact moment for each coordinate, then uses the Euclidean squared-norm formula and linearity of integration over a finite sum. Coordinate independence is unnecessary because that formula contains only coordinate squares.

declarations.name: gaussian_vector_toLp_norm_sq
declarations.title: The Gaussian vector as an L² class
declarations.statement:
Let \([X]\) be the \(L^2\) equivalence class constructed from \(X\), whose coordinates have laws \(\mathcal N(0,v)\). Then

\[\|[X]\|_{L^2}^2=dv.\]

steps.prose: Express the squared \(L^2\) norm as the self-inner-product, then use the definition of the \(L^2\) inner product as an integral.
steps.note: Line 56. rw [← real_inner_self_eq_norm_sq, L2.inner_def] converts the squared L² norm to a self-inner-product and then expresses that L² inner product as an integral of pointwise inner products. The arrow ← reverses the usual direction of the first equality: the library theorem normally states inner ℝ z z = ‖z‖ ^ 2, but here we replace the square by the inner product. L2.inner_def then unfolds the relevant inner-product formula. The ℝ parameter in inner ℝ specifies real scalars. The goal is now an integral involving the representative of the L² class, so it is close to the second-moment theorem but not yet literally its integrand.

steps.prose: The chosen representative of \([X]\) equals \(X\) almost everywhere. Therefore the integrand \(\langle[X](\omega),[X](\omega)\rangle\) agrees almost everywhere with \(\|X(\omega)\|^2\), so the two integrals agree.
steps.note:
Line 57. have hid : ... announces an equality between two integrals. Its left integrand begins with inner ℝ, taking the inner product over the real numbers.

Line 58. The first vector argument is the chosen representative of the class (gaussian_vector_memLp P X v hlaw).toLp X, evaluated at ω. Parentheses first collect the membership proof so .toLp X can construct the class.

Line 59. The second vector argument is the same representative. After ∂P, the equality compares this self-inner-product integral with ∫ ω, ‖X ω‖ ^ 2 ∂P. := by starts the subproof of hid; line wrapping does not change the applications.

Line 60. apply integral_congr_ae reduces equality of the integrals to equality of their integrands almost everywhere. This theorem is the appropriate tool because equality of representatives may fail on a null set without changing either integral.

Line 61. .coeFn_toLp proves that the representative created by .toLp X agrees with X almost everywhere. filter_upwards [thatProof] with ω hω moves to a generic outcome ω in the full-measure set where this equality holds, and names the pointwise equality hω. The square-bracket list gives the almost-everywhere premises to combine; with names the outcome and their pointwise versions.

Line 62. rw [hω, real_inner_self_eq_norm_sq] first substitutes X ω for the representative in both inner-product inputs, then replaces its self-inner-product by ‖X ω‖ ^ 2. The pointwise goal is now an identity, completing the almost-everywhere equality and the local integral identity hid.

steps.prose: Substitute the integral identity and the vector second-moment calculation \(\int\|X\|^2\,dP=dv\).
steps.note: Line 63. rw [hid, gaussian_vector_second_moment P X v hlaw] performs two final replacements. The first changes the representative-based inner-product integral to the integral of the actual vector’s squared norm. The second invokes the previously proved exact vector moment for the same measure, function, variance, and law proofs. Function application is by spaces, so P X v hlaw are four arguments, not one compound symbol. After these rewrites the two sides are the same real expression d * v, and rw finishes the goal by reflexivity. The result therefore concerns the genuine L² norm of the quotient class, with the representative issue fully justified.

declarations.statement_note: Lines 53–55 retain X, v, and the coordinate-law proof. The expression gaussian_vector_memLp P X v hlaw is a proof that the ordinary function X is square integrable. .toLp X uses that proof to construct the corresponding element of Lp (E d) 2 P, the quotient space where functions equal almost everywhere count as the same element. Thus ‖(...).toLp X‖ is a single L² norm; its square is the second moment. The conclusion identifies it with d * v. Evaluating an Lp element at ω uses a chosen representative, so its values need only agree with the original X almost everywhere. The proof explicitly handles this representative issue rather than asserting equality at every outcome.

declarations.name: gaussian_vector_toLp_norm
declarations.title: The square-root Gaussian norm
declarations.statement:
For the same Gaussian coordinate laws,

\[\|[X]\|_{L^2}=\sqrt{dv}.\]

This includes \(d=0\) and \(v=0\).

steps.prose: Replace \(dv\) by \(\|[X]\|^2\). Since norms are nonnegative, \(\sqrt{\|[X]\|^2}=\|[X]\|\).
steps.note: Line 69. The first rule in rw [← gaussian_vector_toLp_norm_sq P X v hlaw, ...] is our previous theorem in reverse. It replaces the product d * v inside the square root by the square of the L² norm on the left. The arrow ← means “use this equality from right to left”; it is unrelated to a function-type arrow. Real.sqrt_sq (norm_nonneg _) then replaces the square root of that squared norm by the norm itself. norm_nonneg _ proves the needed sign condition for the particular L² class; the underscore asks Lean to infer that class from context. The final goal has identical sides and closes. This is an exact symbolic square-root calculation, with no estimate or rounding.

declarations.statement_note: Lines 66–68 state the unsquared version of the previous result, using the same ambient sample space, measure, dimension, vector, variance, and coordinate laws. The left side is the L² norm of the class created using the membership proof. The right side is Real.sqrt ((d : ℝ) * (v : ℝ)). Real.sqrt is nonnegative, and a norm is also nonnegative, which determines the sign when passing from an equality of squares to an equality of values. Neither d nor v is required to be nonzero. The proof uses a rewrite of the squared norm followed by a square-root identity; it does not divide by the norm, so the zero cases are included automatically.

declarations.name: gaussian_vector_scaled_l2_norm
declarations.title: Include the Langevin diffusion factor
declarations.statement:
If every coordinate of \(X\) has law \(\mathcal N(0,v)\), then the Langevin-scaled vector satisfies

\[\|\sqrt2[X]\|_{L^2}=\sqrt{2d}\sqrt v.\]

steps.prose: Norm homogeneity gives \(\|\sqrt2[X]\|=\sqrt2\|[X]\|\), because \(\sqrt2\ge0\). Insert \(\|[X]\|=\sqrt{dv}\), then split the square roots of the nonnegative products.
steps.note:
Line 76. rw [ begins one rewrite command continuing through line 79. norm_smul gives ‖c • z‖ = ‖c‖ * ‖z‖. Real.norm_eq_abs turns the real scalar norm into absolute value, and abs_of_nonneg (Real.sqrt_nonneg _) removes the absolute value because square roots are nonnegative. The underscore is inferred as the number 2.

Line 77. gaussian_vector_toLp_norm P X v hlaw replaces the unscaled L² norm by sqrt (d * v), applying the earlier theorem to exactly the present data. Its arguments include the proof hlaw, illustrating that Lean theorem applications can take proofs as arguments alongside functions and numbers.

Line 78. Real.sqrt_mul (by positivity : (0 : ℝ) ≤ d) splits the product under sqrt (d * v). The small typed proof confirms that the natural-number dimension, coerced to a real, is nonnegative. Here positivity proves a sign condition; it does not numerically evaluate the dimension.

Line 79. Real.sqrt_mul (by norm_num : (0 : ℝ) ≤ 2) also splits sqrt (2 * d) on the other side, using the concrete sign of two. The closing bracket ends the rewrite list. The remaining goal has the same factors, possibly in different order or with different parentheses.

steps.prose: Rearrange \(\sqrt2\sqrt d\sqrt v\) into \(\sqrt{2d}\sqrt v\).
steps.note: Line 80. ring completes the scalar product rearrangement. After the square-root product identities have been explicitly applied, each square-root expression can be treated as an ordinary real factor. The tactic therefore proves the equality by commutative-ring algebra, not by calculating an approximate square root. Together with norm_smul, this establishes the exact Langevin noise scale in L². The proof also covers zero dimension and zero variance: no inverse, division by a variable, or positive-variance condition was used.

declarations.statement_note: Lines 72–75 introduce the Langevin diffusion factor. Real.sqrt 2 • ... multiplies the L² vector class by the real scalar square root of two. The • is scalar multiplication in the L² space, while the * on the right multiplies real numbers. The conclusion writes the scaled norm as sqrt (2 * d) * sqrt v. The same coordinate-law hypothesis supplies all required integrability; it is not necessary to re-prove MemLp for a separate raw scaled function because scalar multiplication is already an operation on L² elements. The proof uses homogeneity of the norm and the exact unscaled Gaussian norm, then rearranges square-root factors. All types and coercions are explicit where a natural or nonnegative real becomes a real scalar.

declarations.name: brownianVector
declarations.title: Assemble Brownian coordinates
declarations.statement:
For scalar processes \(W_i:[0,\infty)\times\Omega\to\mathbb R\), define the Euclidean vector

\[W_t(\omega):=(W_0(t,\omega),\ldots,W_{d-1}(t,\omega))\in E_d.\]

steps.prose: Collect the coordinates at the fixed time \(t\) and outcome \(\omega\), using the finite-dimensional \(\ell^2\) norm.
steps.note: Line 84. fun ω ↦ ... returns a function of the outcome ω. Inside it, fun i ↦ W i t ω forms the coordinate tuple at the fixed time and outcome. These are nested lambda expressions: neither arrow is a proof implication. WithLp.toLp 2 views that finite coordinate function as a vector with the Euclidean, or exponent-two, norm, giving an element of E d. This finite-dimensional type conversion is different from MemLp.toLp, which constructs an equivalence class of random functions using a membership proof. Here no measure P appears and no almost-everywhere quotient is constructed; the output is one actual vector at each ω. Spaces denote application: W i t ω means ((W i) t) ω, and the parentheses keep the coordinate lambda together as one input to WithLp.toLp 2.

declarations.statement_note: Line 83 is a definition, not a theorem. W : Fin d → ℝ≥0 → Ω → ℝ is a family of scalar processes. Function arrows associate to the right: first supply a coordinate i, then a nonnegative time t, then an outcome ω, obtaining a real number W i t ω. The next explicit parameter (t : ℝ≥0) fixes a time, and the result type Ω → E d says the definition returns a random vector, still waiting for an outcome. The := introduces the defining lambda on line 84. There is no pre-Brownian-law assumption in this definition: it can assemble any such family of functions into vectors. Distributional properties will be proved under hypotheses afterwards.

declarations.name: brownianVector_coordinate_law
declarations.title: Brownian marginals are Gaussian
declarations.statement:
Assume each scalar \(W_i\) satisfies \(\mathrm{IsPreBrownianReal}\) under \(P\). For each \(t\ge0\) and coordinate \(i\),

\[W_t^{(i)}\sim\mathcal N(0,t).\]

steps.prose: Apply the scalar Brownian marginal-law theorem at time \(t\). The \(i\)-th coordinate of the assembled vector is definitionally the original scalar process.
steps.note: Line 90. hW i applies the universal pre-Brownian hypothesis to the selected coordinate. The resulting proof concerns the scalar process W i. .hasLaw_eval t invokes the library theorem giving its distribution at the time t: centered Gaussian with variance t. The result is already a proof of the required proposition. Although the conclusion displays brownianVector W t ω i, Lean can reduce the vector-assembly definition and see that it is the same scalar coordinate as W i t ω; this is definitional equality, requiring no separate rewrite theorem. The dot notation supplies the pre-Brownian proof as an input to hasLaw_eval, while the space before t supplies the time argument. This line uses a marginal law, so it does not require independence among different coordinates.

declarations.statement_note: Lines 87–89 take a coordinate-process family W and a proof hW : ∀ i, IsPreBrownianReal (W i) P. For every coordinate, this asserts mathlib’s pre-Brownian finite-dimensional laws; continuity of paths is not required for the marginal calculation. (t : ℝ≥0) is a fixed nonnegative time and (i : Fin d) a fixed coordinate. The conclusion HasLaw (fun ω ↦ brownianVector W t ω i) (gaussianReal 0 t) P says that coordinate at time t has centered Gaussian law of variance t, including its almost-everywhere measurability. The definition of brownianVector makes this coordinate exactly W i t ω. After :=, the proof below is an existing theorem applied directly; a tactic block is unnecessary.

declarations.name: brownianVector_memLp
declarations.title: Brownian vectors belong to L²
declarations.statement:
Under the scalar pre-Brownian assumptions, for every \(t\ge0\),

\[W_t\in L^2(P;E_d).\]

steps.prose: Apply Gaussian vector square integrability with variance \(v=t\), using the just-proved marginal laws of all coordinates.
steps.note: Line 96. Read gaussian_vector_memLp P (brownianVector W t) t (...) as an application of the Gaussian vector theorem with four explicit inputs: the measure P, the vector-valued function brownianVector W t, the variance t, and a proof of its coordinate laws. The time t : ℝ≥0 has exactly the type needed for a nonnegative variance. The last parenthesized expression, brownianVector_coordinate_law P W hW t, supplies that proof for all coordinates; it still awaits a coordinate argument, matching the theorem’s ∀ i requirement. Parentheses group a multiword application into one input. This entire line is a proof term of the stated MemLp proposition after :=, so no by, apply, or exact is needed.

declarations.statement_note: Lines 93–95 take W, coordinate-wise pre-Brownian proofs hW, and a nonnegative time t. brownianVector W t is a function from outcomes to Euclidean vectors. The conclusion MemLp (brownianVector W t) 2 P asserts square integrability of this ordinary vector-valued function under P. It does not yet choose an L² equivalence class. The measure P is the explicit ambient parameter declared on line 22 and must be supplied to Gaussian moment theorems. The proof term on line 96 reuses two already established results: Brownian coordinates have the required Gaussian marginal law, and Gaussian coordinate laws imply square integrability of the vector.

declarations.name: brownianVector_scaled_l2_norm
declarations.title: The exact Brownian noise norm
declarations.statement:
For scalar pre-Brownian coordinates and \(t\ge0\),

\[\|\sqrt2[W_t]\|_{L^2}=\sqrt{2d}\sqrt t.\]

steps.prose: Specialize the scaled Gaussian vector norm to the Brownian vector, whose coordinate variance is \(t\). This derives the square-root noise scale from the Brownian laws.
steps.note:
Line 103. gaussian_vector_scaled_l2_norm P (brownianVector W t) t applies the already proved scaled Gaussian norm identity to the Brownian vector at time t, using variance t. This is the proof term following :=, and its final law-proof argument comes on the next line. The expression returns an equality of real norms once all its arguments are supplied.

Line 104. (brownianVector_coordinate_law P W hW t) supplies the family of Gaussian coordinate laws required by that theorem. The coordinate argument is intentionally omitted because the target is a universal coordinate statement; Lean accepts the partially applied theorem as a function of that coordinate. The membership proofs displayed in the theorem statement and inside the Gaussian result lead to the same L² class, so the supplied equality matches the stated goal. Line wrapping merely makes the long application readable; it does not create a second tactic or a separate claim.

declarations.statement_note: Lines 99–102 state the exact norm of the Langevin-scaled Brownian vector at time t. The proof brownianVector_memLp P W hW t establishes L² membership, and .toLp (brownianVector W t) constructs the associated L² class. The outer Real.sqrt 2 • ... scales this class, and the norm is the L² norm. The right side sqrt (2 * d) * sqrt t depends on elapsed time and dimension, with coercions to ℝ displayed. The only probabilistic input is hW, asserting scalar pre-Brownian laws coordinate by coordinate. The theorem does not introduce a coupled Langevin process or claim stationarity; it provides precisely the Brownian noise moment used by the later conditional analytic argument.

declarations.name: brownianVectorIncrement
declarations.title: Define an increment from any starting time
declarations.statement:
For \(a,t\ge0\), define the vector increment over the interval \([a,a+t]\) by

\[\Delta_aW_t(\omega):=W_{a+t}(\omega)-W_a(\omega).\]

steps.prose: Subtract the two Euclidean vectors at the interval endpoints. Each coordinate is the corresponding scalar Brownian increment.
steps.note: Line 108. fun ω ↦ ... defines the increment pointwise at an outcome. brownianVector W (a + t) ω is the vector at the ending time; brownianVector W a ω is the vector at the starting time. The minus sign subtracts these actual Euclidean vectors. Because the subtraction is pointwise in the sample outcome, the resulting random function has coordinates W i (a + t) ω - W i a ω. Parentheses around (a + t) make the whole sum one time argument; without grouping, function application would have a different parse. This definition uses neither integration nor an L² quotient, so the equality holds as a direct vector formula at every outcome. Its square integrability will be deduced later from the distribution of each scalar increment.

declarations.statement_note: Line 107 defines a random vector increment. W is again the coordinate family, while (a t : ℝ≥0) introduces two nonnegative real inputs with the same type. The intended starting time is a, and t is elapsed time. The result type Ω → E d says the definition returns a random vector function. The operation a + t is addition inside nonnegative reals; no proof that it is nonnegative is needed because the type already carries that property. The := introduces the expression on line 108. No law assumption is needed to define a difference of vectors; Gaussian laws and moments are separate theorems that impose hW afterwards.

declarations.name: brownianVectorIncrement_coordinate_law
declarations.title: Increment variance is elapsed time
declarations.statement:
Under the scalar pre-Brownian assumptions, for every \(a,t\ge0\) and every coordinate \(i\),

\[W_i(a+t)-W_i(a)\sim\mathcal N(0,t).\]

steps.prose: Expand the vector increment to its scalar coordinate. Apply the Brownian difference-law theorem at times \(a+t\) and \(a\); its variance is the nonnegative distance between those times.
steps.note:
Line 115. change HasLaw ... replaces the goal by a definitionally equal version using the scalar expression W i (a + t) ω - W i a ω. change is not a new assumption: Lean verifies that unfolding brownianVectorIncrement, brownianVector, and coordinate operations gives exactly this proposition. It makes the form match the existing scalar Brownian law theorem.

Line 116. (hW i).hasLaw_sub (a + t) a is the known law for the difference at these two times. convert ... using 1 attempts to use that proof, while leaving equalities between the target and theorem parameters as new goals. The 1 is a structural comparison depth, not a number of time units or a probability. Here the outstanding issue is the variance: the theorem has nonnegative endpoint distance, while we require t.

steps.prose:
It remains to identify that variance. As real numbers,

\[|(a+t)-a|=|t|=t,\]

because \(t\ge0\). Thus the increment law is exactly \(\mathcal N(0,t)\).
steps.note:
Line 117. congr 1 reduces equality of the Gaussian-law expressions to equality of their variance inputs, looking through one level of their shared constructor/function application. This is a congruence step: equal inputs give equal outputs.

Line 118. apply NNReal.eq uses the fact that two nonnegative reals are equal if their underlying real values are equal. The new goal is thus an ordinary real equality, where subtraction and absolute values are easier to simplify.

Line 119. simp only [coe_nndist, Real.dist_eq] views the nonnegative distance as the ordinary real distance and then writes real distance as an absolute difference. only restricts the rules, keeping the ensuing expression explicit.

Line 120. change (t : ℝ) = |((a : ℝ) + (t : ℝ)) - (a : ℝ)| presents the same real equality after coercing the times. The vertical bars |...| mean absolute value. These are not the doubled norm bars ‖...‖ used for vectors.

Line 121. rw [add_sub_cancel_left, abs_of_nonneg t.coe_nonneg] cancels a in (a + t) - a, then uses the nonnegative-real type’s proof t.coe_nonneg to turn |t| into t. The remaining identity closes the variance goal, allowing convert to complete the desired law proof.

declarations.statement_note: Lines 112–114 take the coordinate family W, the pre-Brownian-law proof family hW, two nonnegative times a and t, and a coordinate i : Fin d. The conclusion is a law assertion: the ith coordinate of the vector increment over [a,a+t] is centered Gaussian with variance t. HasLaw includes almost-everywhere measurability as well as the equality of pushforward measures. The subtle point is that the library difference-law theorem writes the variance as the nonnegative distance between the endpoint times. Our statement writes it as elapsed time. The proof therefore applies that library law and then proves equality of those two nonnegative-real variance parameters. It works at any starting time and also permits t = 0.

declarations.name: brownianVectorIncrement_memLp
declarations.title: Increments are square integrable
declarations.statement:
For pre-Brownian coordinates and any \(a,t\ge0\),

\[\Delta_aW_t\in L^2(P;E_d).\]

steps.prose: Each increment coordinate has the centered Gaussian law of variance \(t\), so the Gaussian vector integrability theorem applies.
steps.note:
Line 127. gaussian_vector_memLp P (brownianVectorIncrement W a t) t applies the general Gaussian-coordinate integrability theorem, supplying the measure, the increment random-vector function, and the nonnegative variance t. The entire parenthesized expression is one function argument; the starting time a is already fixed inside it. This line continues the proof term begun after := on line 126.

Line 128. (brownianVectorIncrement_coordinate_law P W hW a t) supplies the last argument: a proof of the centered Gaussian variance-t law for every coordinate of the increment. It is partially applied without a final coordinate index because the required argument itself has the type ∀ i, .... After this argument, the application produces exactly the MemLp proof declared in the statement. No tactical exact is needed when a declaration’s body is already a proof term.

declarations.statement_note: Lines 124–126 take the same pre-Brownian family and the nonnegative starting and elapsed times. The conclusion MemLp (brownianVectorIncrement W a t) 2 P says the actual increment function is square integrable. It is a proposition about that function, not a new definition of the increment and not yet an L² class. The previous coordinate-law theorem has exactly the form required by gaussian_vector_memLp, with the variance set to elapsed time t. The theorem therefore needs no separate norm estimate to establish membership, and needs no independence among coordinates. The measure and dimension remain the common ambient parameters from line 22.

declarations.name: brownianVector_increment_scaled_l2_norm
declarations.title: The same noise norm on every reference segment
declarations.statement:
For scalar pre-Brownian coordinates and every \(a,t\ge0\),

\[\boxed{\|\sqrt2[W_{a+t}-W_a]\|_{L^2}=\sqrt{2d}\sqrt t.}\]

steps.prose: Apply the scaled Gaussian vector norm to the increment coordinate laws. The answer depends only on elapsed time \(t\), so every reference interval has the same moment bound.
steps.note:
Line 137. gaussian_vector_scaled_l2_norm P (brownianVectorIncrement W a t) t specializes the exact scaled Gaussian norm theorem to the increment function and variance t. The starting time a enters only through the chosen random function, not the variance. This is an ordinary theorem application used as the complete declaration body after the final argument on line 138.

Line 138. (brownianVectorIncrement_coordinate_law P W hW a t) is that final law-proof argument, a function supplying the correct Gaussian law at each coordinate. Once it is given, the general theorem returns the desired equality with sqrt (2 * d) * sqrt t. The proof uses the exact law and the already checked Gaussian moments, rather than assuming an L² noise bound as a separate hypothesis. This completes the probabilistic ingredient used for each interval of the reference process.

declarations.statement_note: Lines 132–136 state the exact L² norm of the increment multiplied by sqrt 2. brownianVectorIncrement_memLp P W hW a t is the membership proof used to construct its class with .toLp (brownianVectorIncrement W a t). Parentheses group the raw increment function as one .toLp argument; its outcome variable is not supplied because an L² class is made from the whole random function. The outer norm is the norm on this function space. The right side contains t but not a, expressing dependence only on elapsed time. The hypotheses are the actual coordinate-wise pre-Brownian laws. Their existence is assumed here; the result extracts the moment consequence for any such supplied family.

sections.setup_note:
Lines 1–4 import this project’s Euclidean-space definitions and mathlib’s Brownian-motion, finite-dimensional Lp, and L² inner-product results. Line 15 starts a noncomputable section: abstract integrals and equivalence-class representatives are permitted even without an executable algorithm. Lines 17–18 open namespaces MeasureTheory and ProbabilityTheory and the scoped nonnegative-real notation. open shortens names already defined by imports; it does not prove a result. Line 20 begins namespace ULA. Line 22 declares the common parameters: {Ω : Type*} is an implicit sample-space type, [MeasurableSpace Ω] specifies which subsets are measurable, (P : Measure Ω) is an explicit measure, and {d : ℕ} is an implicit natural-number dimension. Brackets around MeasurableSpace Ω request an automatically supplied typeclass instance.

The project notation E d means real Euclidean space of dimension d, represented using mathlib’s finite-dimensional WithLp construction. Fin d is the finite index type with values 0 through d - 1; it is empty when d = 0. An expression X ω i first evaluates the random vector at outcome ω, then its coordinate at i.
