A law assertion HasLaw X μ P includes almost-everywhere measurability and the identity P.map X = μ: pushing the measure P through X produces μ. No coordinate-independence hypothesis occurs here. Also distinguish MemLp X 2 P, a proposition about an ordinary function X, from Lp (E d) 2 P, the type of square-integrable functions modulo equality almost everywhere. See probability syntax.

sections.title: The actual gradient on square-integrable random variables
sections.intro:
Let \(P\) be a finite measure on \(\Omega\). The first five results need only a normed additive commutative group \(H\); all Lipschitz constants \(L\) are nonnegative. When \(H\) is a real Banach space, \(L^2(P;H)\) provides the Banach space needed for the local-defect estimate. For a Lipschitz vector field \(g:H\to H\), construct the operator \(\mathcal G[X]=[g\circ X]\), including the case \(g(0)\ne0\). Finiteness of \(P\) ensures the constant offset is square integrable.

The gradient results use a real Hilbert space \(H\). The two score-moment lemmas need only a real inner-product space, without completeness. Whenever \(g=\nabla U\), this is the potential’s actual gradient, and the resulting \(L^2\) recursion is proved to represent the original pointwise ULA chain.

declarations.name: centered_lipschitz
declarations.title: Center a Lipschitz vector field
declarations.statement:
In a normed additive group \(H\), if \(g:H\to H\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz, then so is

\[\widetilde g(x):=g(x)-g(0).\]

steps.prose:
For arbitrary \(x,y\), the common offset cancels:

\[\|\widetilde g(x)-\widetilde g(y)\|=\|g(x)-g(y)\|\le L\|x-y\|.\]

This is precisely the required Lipschitz inequality.
steps.note:
Line 28. apply LipschitzWith.of_dist_le_mul works backwards from the desired Lipschitz property: it is enough to show that every pair of outputs has distance at most L times the input distance. apply leaves that quantified distance bound as the new goal rather than proving it immediately.

Line 29. intro x y fixes arbitrary points in H, the two universally quantified inputs. The goal now concerns the distance between g x - g 0 and g y - g 0. These names denote vectors, not hypotheses.

Line 30. hLip.dist_le_mul x y is the supplied Lipschitz estimate for g at the same points. simpa only [dist_eq_norm, sub_sub_sub_cancel_right] using ... rewrites distances as norms of differences and cancels the common g 0 inside those differences. The proposition of the existing proof then matches the target for the centered map. simpa combines simplification with reuse of a proof; the square brackets list rules, and only makes that list explicit and controlled. This finishes the Lipschitz proof for all pairs of points.

declarations.statement_note: Lines 26–27 take an implicit nonnegative constant {L : ℝ≥0}, an implicit function {g : H → H}, and an explicit proof hLip : LipschitzWith L g. The conclusion is another Lipschitz proposition, for fun x ↦ g x - g 0 with the same constant L. The lambda defines a new function by subtracting the fixed vector g 0 from every output. Here 0 is the zero vector in H, inferred from the input type of g. The ambient assumptions at this point require only the normed additive group, together with the sample-space measure setting that will be used in later declarations. The proof uses the distance characterization of Lipschitz continuity and cancellation of that common output offset.

declarations.name: lpDrift
declarations.title: Construct the lifted drift
declarations.statement:
Let \(P\) be finite and \(g\) be \(L\)-Lipschitz. For \(X\in L^2(P;H)\), define

\[\mathcal G[X]:=[\widetilde g\circ X]+[g(0)].\]

steps.prose: The centered function satisfies \(\widetilde g(0)=0\) and \(\|\widetilde g(x)\|\le L\|x\|\), so composition produces an \(L^2\) class. Add the constant class \([g(0)]\), which belongs to \(L^2\) because \(P\) is finite.
steps.note: Line 36. centered_lipschitz hLip proves that the function x ↦ g x - g 0 is Lipschitz. Its .compLp operation constructs composition on L² equivalence classes. The argument (by simp) proves that this centered function sends zero to zero: its value is g 0 - g 0 = 0. This is a small proof argument, not a value added to the class. The next argument X is the class to compose with. Lp.const 2 P (g 0) constructs the constant L² class with value g 0, using the ambient finiteness of P. Finally + adds the two L² elements. The definition therefore represents (g (X ω) - g 0) + g 0, but the representative identity will be proved almost everywhere next. The number 2 is the Lp exponent in both constructions; it is not a coordinate index.

declarations.statement_note: Lines 34–35 define a map on L² classes from an ordinary Lipschitz vector field g : H → H. {L : ℝ≥0} is inferred from the supplied proof hLip, while (X : Lp H 2 P) is an L² element. The final : Lp H 2 P is the output type, and := starts its defining expression. Direct Lipschitz composition in the library expects the vector field to send zero to zero. The map g need not do so, which is why the definition composes with g x - g 0 first and adds back the constant. The ambient finite-measure assumption makes this added constant an L² element. P is an explicit ambient parameter, hence later applications write lpDrift P g hLip X.

declarations.name: lpDrift_coe
declarations.title: The lift agrees with the original vector field
declarations.statement:
For finite \(P\), Lipschitz \(g\), and \(X\in L^2(P;H)\),

\[\mathcal G[X](\omega)=g(X(\omega))\quad\text{for }P\text{-almost every }\omega.\]

steps.prose: Expand \(\mathcal G\) into the centered composition class plus the constant class.
steps.note: Line 41. unfold lpDrift expands the defined L² drift into its centered composition plus constant class. The goal remains equality almost everywhere; unfolding only reveals the construction whose representative is being compared. It does not assert that every representative operation is pointwise at every outcome. The following filter_upwards command will supply the valid pointwise identities on a full-measure set. See almost-everywhere equality for the role of =ᵐ[P].

steps.prose: Intersect the full-measure sets on which the representative of the sum, the composition, and the constant class agree with their pointwise formulas.
steps.note:
Line 42. filter_upwards [ begins a list of almost-everywhere equalities to use together. Lp.coeFn_add supplies the representative formula for adding two L² classes. Its first argument is the centered-composition class; the second argument follows on line 43. The command will reduce the almost-everywhere goal to a pointwise proof where all these equalities hold.

Line 43. Lp.const 2 P (g 0) is the second addend, completing the arguments to Lp.coeFn_add. The comma separates this first almost-everywhere premise from the next one; it is not tuple construction.

Line 44. (centered_lipschitz hLip).coeFn_compLp (by simp) X supplies the representative formula for the centered composition. Again (by simp) proves the zero-preserving condition of the centered map. This premise identifies its representative with pointwise composition almost everywhere.

Line 45. Lp.coeFn_const (μ := P) (p := 2) (c := g 0) supplies the constant-class representative formula, with named arguments for measure, exponent, and constant value. with ω hadd hcomp hconst then names a generic outcome and the three pointwise equalities obtained from the three premises. The main task is now an ordinary vector equality at such an ω, on their common full-measure set.

steps.prose: On this set the value is \((g(X(\omega))-g(0))+g(0)\). Cancel the offset to recover \(g(X(\omega))\).
steps.note:
Line 46. simp only [hadd, hcomp, hconst, ...] substitutes the representative formulas into the pointwise goal. The remaining library rules Function.comp_apply, Pi.add_apply, and Function.const_apply evaluate a composed function, a sum of functions at an argument, and a constant function at an argument. Pi is the namespace for pointwise function operations; it is not the probability symbol π. This exposes the ordinary vector expression (g (X ω) - g 0) + g 0.

Line 47. exact sub_add_cancel _ _ proves the last cancellation, (a - b) + b = a, with Lean inferring a = g (X ω) and b = g 0 for the underscores. Here _ supplies inferred arguments, not missing proof obligations. Since the equality was established on the full-measure set from filter_upwards, it finishes the original almost-everywhere statement.

declarations.statement_note: Lines 39–40 use the same data as the definition and assert its representative formula. lpDrift P g hLip X =ᵐ[P] fun ω ↦ g (X ω) means that the chosen representative of the L² output agrees with pointwise application of g, outside a P-null set. Lean automatically views the Lp element on the left as a function for this comparison. The right lambda is an ordinary random-vector function, rather than an L² class. This distinction matters: quotient-space addition and composition are compatible with pointwise formulas almost everywhere, but arbitrary representatives need not satisfy them at every individual outcome. The proof combines those almost-everywhere formulas before cancelling the centered offset.

declarations.name: lpDrift_memLp
declarations.title: The actual pointwise drift is square integrable
declarations.statement:
For finite \(P\), Lipschitz \(g\), and \(X\in L^2(P;H)\),

\[g\circ X\in L^2(P;H).\]

steps.prose: The constructed class \(\mathcal G[X]\) has an \(L^2\) representative. Transfer its square integrability to \(g\circ X\) using their almost-everywhere equality.
steps.note: Line 52. Lp.memLp (lpDrift P g hLip X) says the chosen representative of our constructed L² element has MemLp membership. The surrounding parentheses group that proof so .ae_eq can be called on it. .ae_eq (lpDrift_coe P g hLip X) transfers the membership property to the ordinary pointwise drift using the almost-everywhere equality from the preceding theorem. This is legitimate because changing a function on a null set does not change its Lp membership. The result is a proof of MemLp (fun ω ↦ g (X ω)) 2 P, exactly the declared conclusion. As this is a direct proof term after :=, there is no tactic block and no exact keyword; the expression itself has the required proposition as its type.

declarations.statement_note: Lines 50–51 state square integrability of the ordinary pointwise function fun ω ↦ g (X ω). We already have an L² element representing this function, namely lpDrift P g hLip X. However, MemLp is a proposition about the actual function, whereas Lp H 2 P is the type of equivalence classes. The theorem bridges those two statements using the almost-everywhere representative identity just proved. The data are a finite measure, a Lipschitz field, and an L² input, with no zero-at-origin assumption. The finite measure makes the constant part integrable; this is why the assertion works even when g 0 ≠ 0.

declarations.name: lpDrift_lipschitz
declarations.title: The drift keeps its Lipschitz constant in L²
declarations.statement:
For finite \(P\) and \(L\)-Lipschitz \(g\), the lifted drift is \(L\)-Lipschitz:

\[\|\mathcal G[X]-\mathcal G[Y]\|_{L^2}\le L\|X-Y\|_{L^2}.\]

steps.prose: Fix \(X,Y\). The two constant classes cancel in their drift difference. For the remaining centered compositions, the pointwise Lipschitz estimate passes to the \(L^2\) norm, giving the same constant \(L\).
steps.note:
Line 57. apply LipschitzWith.of_dist_le_mul reduces the Lipschitz claim to a distance inequality for every two inputs. This is the same characterization used for ordinary vectors, now in the normed space of L² classes.

Line 58. intro X Y fixes two arbitrary L² elements. The goal compares the distance between their lifted drifts with L times their own distance.

Line 59. simp only [lpDrift, dist_eq_norm, add_sub_add_right_eq_sub] unfolds lpDrift, replaces distances by norms of differences, and cancels the identical constant class Lp.const 2 P (g 0) from the difference. A defined name such as lpDrift in a simplification list asks simplification to unfold its defining expression, whereas a proved lemma in the same list rewrites by its conclusion. What remains involves only the centered-composition classes.

Line 60. (centered_lipschitz hLip).norm_compLp_sub_le (by simp) X Y gives precisely the remaining norm inequality for the centered map’s composition operator. The short proof supplies the zero-preserving condition; X and Y are the two L² inputs. exact closes the goal with this existing verified inequality.

declarations.statement_note: Lines 55–56 assert that the map lpDrift P g hLip, regarded as a function from Lp H 2 P to itself, is Lipschitz with constant L. The input class argument is intentionally not supplied in this expression: partial application leaves a function waiting for a class. The ordinary field g is given together with proof hLip; the measure P is finite. The theorem is a property of the entire lifted map, rather than a statement at one particular random variable. Its proof fixes two L² inputs, expands the definition, cancels the common constant class, and uses the library’s norm inequality for zero-preserving Lipschitz composition.

declarations.name: lpDrift_gradient_contract
declarations.title: Lift the small-step gradient contraction
declarations.statement:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, \(P\) finite, and \(U:H\to\mathbb R\) differentiable and \(m\)-strongly convex on \(H\), with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient. Assume \(m\le L\), \(m+L>0\), and \(0\le h\le2/(m+L)\). Write \(\mathcal G[X]=[\nabla U\circ X]\). Then, for all \(X,Y\in L^2(P;H)\),

\[\|(X-h\mathcal G[X])-(Y-h\mathcal G[Y])\|_{L^2}\le(1-mh)\|X-Y\|_{L^2}.\]

steps.prose: It suffices to prove the corresponding norm inequality almost everywhere between representatives: integrating the squared pointwise inequality gives the \(L^2\) bound.
steps.note: Line 74. apply Lp.norm_le_mul_norm_of_ae_le_mul replaces the requested L² norm inequality by an almost-everywhere inequality between the pointwise norms of the corresponding representatives. Lean infers the two L² elements and the scalar factor 1 - m * h by matching the theorem conclusion to the goal. The resulting goal has the form ∀ᵐ ω ∂P, ..., meaning it must hold outside a null set. We can then use the deterministic contraction theorem at each such outcome. This library step handles passage from representative inequalities to L² norms; we do not manually interchange a square, integral, and square root.

steps.prose: Work on a common full-measure set where the outer difference and both Euler-step differences have their ordinary pointwise subtraction formulas.
steps.note:
Line 75. filter_upwards [ starts collecting the almost-everywhere representative formulas needed for the new pointwise inequality. The first premise is Lp.coeFn_sub for the outer difference of the two Euler-step classes.

Line 76. This is the first L² argument to that outer subtraction formula, the step X - h • lpDrift ... X. At this stage it is still an equivalence class, not its expanded value at ω.

Line 77. This is the second argument, the corresponding Y step. The comma completes the first almost-everywhere premise.

Line 78. Lp.coeFn_sub X (h • lpDrift ... X) provides the representative formula for the inner subtraction in the X step.

Line 79. The analogous Lp.coeFn_sub provides the formula for the Y step. These premises are needed separately because the representative of a difference class is only guaranteed to agree almost everywhere with the difference of the chosen representatives. The list continues below; no pointwise proof has started yet.

steps.prose: Also require the scalar multiples, both lifted gradients, and \(X-Y\) to have their pointwise formulas. The two drift terms are then \(\nabla U(X(\omega))\) and \(\nabla U(Y(\omega))\).
steps.note:
Line 80. Lp.coeFn_smul h ... gives the representative formula for scalar multiplication in the X drift term. It identifies the value of the scaled class with h times the value of its representative almost everywhere.

Line 81. The analogous premise handles the Y drift term, using the same real scalar h.

Line 82. The two lpDrift_coe applications identify the lifted drift representatives with the actual pointwise gradients of U at the representatives of X and Y. Their common arguments P (gradient U) hLip supply the measure, field, and its Lipschitz proof.

Line 83. Lp.coeFn_sub X Y supplies the representative formula for the difference on the comparison’s right side. The ] closes the eight-premise list. with ω hsub hX hY hsX hsY hgX hgY hXY names the common outcome and, in list order, all eight pointwise identities. The pointwise goal is now considered where every named identity is valid.

steps.prose:
Substitute these representative identities and apply the deterministic sharp contraction to \(x=X(\omega)\), \(y=Y(\omega)\):

\[\|(x-h\nabla U(x))-(y-h\nabla U(y))\|\le(1-mh)\|x-y\|.\]
steps.note:
Line 84. simp only [...] substitutes all eight representative equalities. Pi.sub_apply and Pi.smul_apply reduce pointwise function subtraction and scalar multiplication when evaluated at ω. The target becomes the deterministic norm estimate for the vectors X ω and Y ω, with actual gradients, rather than a statement about chosen L²-operation representatives.

Line 85. exact strong_smooth_gradient_step_contract U m h L hdiff hsc hLip hmL hpos hh hsmall begins application of the deterministic theorem. It passes the potential, constants, differentiability and convexity proofs, gradient Lipschitz proof, and all numerical regime conditions in declaration order.

Line 86. The final arguments (X ω) (Y ω) select the two actual vectors at this outcome. The obtained deterministic inequality closes the pointwise goal; filter_upwards then establishes it almost everywhere, and line 74’s library theorem gives the desired L² bound. Parentheses keep each evaluated vector together as one input.

declarations.statement_note: Line 62 has added [InnerProductSpace ℝ H] [CompleteSpace H], so the ambient vector space is now real Hilbert. Lines 67–73 take a potential U : H → ℝ, real parameters m and h, and nonnegative Lipschitz constant L. The proofs hdiff, hsc, and hLip assert differentiability of U, strong convexity on Set.univ (the whole space), and Lipschitz continuity of its actual gradient U. The numerical hypotheses hmL, hpos, hh, and hsmall specify m ≤ L, a positive denominator m + L, a nonnegative step, and the small-step regime. X and Y are L² classes. The conclusion bounds the L² distance between their two drift steps by (1 - m * h) * ‖X - Y‖. The proof derives this from the deterministic gradient-step inequality at almost every outcome.

declarations.name: lpDrift_gradient_contract_large
declarations.title: Lift the second step-size regime
declarations.statement:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, \(P\) finite, and \(U\) differentiable, \(m\)-strongly convex, with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient. Assume \(m\le L\), \(m+L>0\), \(h\ge0\), and \(h\ge2/(m+L)\). Then

\[\|(X-h\mathcal G[X])-(Y-h\mathcal G[Y])\|_{L^2}\le(Lh-1)\|X-Y\|_{L^2}.\]

The inequality holds in this whole regime; it is a strict contraction when its factor is less than one.

steps.prose: Reduce the \(L^2\) inequality to its almost-everywhere pointwise counterpart with factor \(Lh-1\).
steps.note: Line 97. apply Lp.norm_le_mul_norm_of_ae_le_mul reduces the L² norm inequality to an almost-everywhere pointwise norm inequality with factor (L : ℝ) * h - 1. The theorem application infers the two L² elements and this scalar factor from the goal. It leaves a goal about representative values outside a null set, which can be proved using the deterministic vector estimate. As in the preceding theorem, this step handles the function-space norm reasoning. It is not an assertion that all representatives satisfy all pointwise operation formulas at every outcome.

steps.prose: Choose a full-measure set on which the outer subtraction and each Euler-step subtraction agree with the pointwise vector formulas.
steps.note:
Line 98. filter_upwards [ begins the combined almost-everywhere argument. Lp.coeFn_sub supplies the pointwise formula for the outer difference of the two Euler-step classes.

Line 99. This line is the first argument to that theorem, the X step class. It is still a class-valued expression awaiting evaluation once the representative identity is used.

Line 100. This is the second argument, the Y step class. The comma completes the first list premise.

Line 101. A second Lp.coeFn_sub supplies the pointwise formula for the subtraction inside the X step.

Line 102. A third Lp.coeFn_sub handles the subtraction inside the Y step. The square-bracket list is continuing; the occurrences of parentheses group arguments of each theorem application rather than starting new statements.

steps.prose: On the same set identify scalar multiplication, both lifted gradient representatives, and the representative of \(X-Y\).
steps.note:
Line 103. Lp.coeFn_smul h ... X supplies the representative formula for the scalar-multiplied lifted drift at X. Its conclusion holds almost everywhere, as required for quotient-space representative operations.

Line 104. The next Lp.coeFn_smul gives the same fact for Y, with the same scalar step size h.

Line 105. The two lpDrift_coe premises identify the two lifted drift representatives with the actual gradients at their corresponding input representatives. These are exactly the pointwise vector fields used in the deterministic theorem.

Line 106. Lp.coeFn_sub X Y handles the right-side difference. The closing ] ends the eight-premise list. with ω hsub hX hY hsX hsY hgX hgY hXY gives names to the outcome and the pointwise identities, in the same order as their premises. They all hold on the common full-measure set used for the remaining argument.

steps.prose:
After substitution, invoke the deterministic second-regime estimate at \(X(\omega),Y(\omega)\):

\[\|(x-h\nabla U(x))-(y-h\nabla U(y))\|\le(Lh-1)\|x-y\|.\]
steps.note:
Line 107. simp only [...] uses all eight local equalities to replace the representative values by ordinary vector operations. Pi.sub_apply and Pi.smul_apply evaluate pointwise function operations. After simplification, the target is exactly the second-regime deterministic inequality at the vectors X ω and Y ω.

Line 108. exact strong_smooth_gradient_step_contract_large U m h L hdiff hsc hLip begins the application of that deterministic theorem, supplying the potential, parameters, and analytic hypotheses. These include proofs as well as mathematical data.

Line 109. hmL hpos hh hlarge supplies the remaining numerical hypotheses; (X ω) (Y ω) supplies the two vectors. The hlarge proof is the one selecting this factor. Once the pointwise inequality is proved, the almost-everywhere machinery and line 97 complete the L² inequality.

declarations.statement_note: Lines 89–96 use the same Hilbert-space setting, finite measure, potential, and two L² classes as the small-step result. hdiff gives differentiability, hsc gives strong convexity on the whole space, and hLip supplies the Lipschitz property of the actual gradient. The numerical proofs hmL, hpos, and hh keep the same meanings, but hlarge : 2 / (m + (L : ℝ)) ≤ h selects the second step-size regime. The conclusion therefore uses the factor (L : ℝ) * h - 1. No upper step bound is present in this statement; the inequality is called a strict contraction only when that factor is below one. The proof transfers the deterministic second-regime inequality to L² by the same representative argument.

declarations.name: lpDrift_localDefect_bound
declarations.title: The local defect for the actual L² gradient
declarations.statement:
Let \(P\) be finite, \(H\) a real Hilbert space, and \(\nabla U\) be \(L\)-Lipschitz. Let \(Y,B:\mathbb R\to L^2(P;H)\), let \(h,d\in\mathbb R\), and assume \(h,d\ge0\), \(Lh\le2\). For every \(0\le t\le h\), suppose

\[\|\mathcal G[Y_t]\|_{L^2}\le\sqrt{Ld},\quad\|B_t\|_{L^2}\le\sqrt{2d}\sqrt t,\quad Y_t-Y_0=-\int_0^t\mathcal G[Y_s]\,ds+B_t.\]

Then

\[\|D_h(\mathcal G,Y)\|_{L^2}\le\frac{33}{20}Lh\sqrt{hd}.\]

steps.prose: Apply the Banach-space local-defect theorem to \(\mathcal G\). Its required Lipschitz property is the one just proved for the actual lifted gradient; the reference equation and moment-scale bounds are the displayed hypotheses.
steps.note:
Line 123. localDefect_dalalyan_bound (lpDrift P (gradient U) hLip) Y B L h d hh hd hstep applies the already proved Banach-space local-defect theorem. Its vector-field argument is the actual lifted gradient, grouped in parentheses as a single function. The ambient Banach space is inferred as Lp H 2 P, while Y and B are its time-dependent curves. The three final arguments on this line provide nonnegative time, nonnegative dimension-scale parameter, and the step restriction. This is a direct proof term, continuing after := from the declaration, rather than a sequence of tactics.

Line 124. (lpDrift_lipschitz P (gradient U) hLip) supplies the remaining Lipschitz proof for this lifted vector field. The arguments hG hB heq then provide exactly the moment-scale and integral-equation hypotheses required by the general theorem. Its conclusion now matches the specialized statement. This line shows why constructing the real lifted gradient and proving its Lipschitz constant was necessary: it makes the earlier abstract theorem applicable to the intended random-variable dynamics.

declarations.statement_note: Lines 113–122 specialize the local-defect estimate to the actual lifted gradient. U is the potential, L : ℝ≥0 its gradient Lipschitz constant, and h and d are real parameters with nonnegativity proofs hh and hd. Y B : ℝ → Lp H 2 P are curves whose values are L² classes. hstep is L * h ≤ 2. The hypotheses hG, hB, and heq give the gradient-norm scale, Brownian-norm scale, and integral equation at every time in Set.Icc 0 h. The defect is localDefect (lpDrift P (gradient U) hLip) Y h: a vector in the Banach space L². The conclusion uses that space’s norm. No strong-convexity assumption is needed for this local bound; the score-moment bound remains a displayed input.

declarations.name: lpDrift_norm_sq
declarations.title: Identify the drift norm with the score moment
declarations.statement:
For finite \(P\), a real inner-product space \(H\), Lipschitz \(g:H\to H\), and \(X\in L^2(P;H)\),

\[\|\mathcal G[X]\|_{L^2}^2=\int_\Omega\|g(X(\omega))\|^2\,dP(\omega).\]

steps.prose: Write the squared \(L^2\) norm as a self-inner-product and expand the \(L^2\) inner product into the integral of the pointwise inner product.
steps.note: Line 131. rw [← real_inner_self_eq_norm_sq, L2.inner_def] rewrites the square of the L² norm as a self-inner-product and then as the integral of pointwise self-inner-products. The arrow reverses the first theorem so a norm square is replaced by an inner product, not the other way around. L2.inner_def is the library’s formula for the real L² inner product. The goal now compares two integrals, but the left one still uses the chosen representative of lpDrift, while the right one uses the actual pointwise function g (X ω). The following almost-everywhere argument reconciles them.

steps.prose: Almost everywhere, \(\mathcal G[X](\omega)=g(X(\omega))\). Replace the representative under the integral and use \(\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2\).
steps.note:
Line 132. apply integral_congr_ae reduces equality of these integrals to equality almost everywhere of their integrands. Integral equality does not require equality on a null set, so this matches the strength of the representative theorem.

Line 133. filter_upwards [lpDrift_coe P g hLip X] with ω hω uses the almost-everywhere formula for the lifted drift. It moves to an outcome ω where that formula holds, naming the pointwise equality hω. The square brackets contain an almost-everywhere premise, not simplification rules in this command.

Line 134. rw [hω, real_inner_self_eq_norm_sq] replaces the lifted representative in both inner-product entries by g (X ω), then identifies its self-inner-product with its squared norm. The pointwise equality closes, hence so does the equality almost everywhere and finally the integral identity. The same bracket syntax now lists rewrite equalities because the command is rw rather than filter_upwards.

declarations.statement_note: The omit [CompleteSpace H] in on line 126 removes the ambient completeness requirement for this declaration; a real inner-product space is enough. Lines 128–130 take a Lipschitz field g : H → H, its proof hLip, and an L² input X. The conclusion identifies the square of the L² norm of the lifted drift with the integral of the squared pointwise norm of g (X ω). The integral is over the measure P, marked by ∂P; the right-side norm is in H, while the left-side norm is in Lp H 2 P. ^ 2 squares the resulting real norm in either case. The result is a general identity for Lipschitz fields; taking g = gradient U later gives the score-moment interpretation.

declarations.name: lpDrift_norm_le_sqrt
declarations.title: A second-moment bound gives the drift bound
declarations.statement:
Under the preceding finite-measure and inner-product assumptions, if

\[\int_\Omega\|g(X(\omega))\|^2\,dP(\omega)\le C,\]

then

\[\|\mathcal G[X]\|_{L^2}\le\sqrt C.\]

For \(g=\nabla U\) and \(C=Ld\), the moment inequality is an explicit input, not a consequence of this lemma.

steps.prose: The norm-square identity turns the assumed moment bound into \(\|\mathcal G[X]\|^2\le C\). Taking the nonnegative square root yields the conclusion.
steps.note: Line 142. lpDrift_norm_sq P g hLip X is the exact identity from the preceding theorem. .trans_le hmoment chains that equality with the supplied moment inequality, yielding ‖lpDrift P g hLip X‖ ^ 2 ≤ C. Dot notation here invokes a theorem combining equality and inequality; it is not numerical field access. Real.le_sqrt_of_sq_le turns this bound on a square into the required upper bound by Real.sqrt C. The nested parentheses make the chained inequality one argument of this library theorem. exact then supplies the resulting proof of the goal. The relation between a second moment and its square-root norm is therefore proved symbolically with the correct real square-root theorem, including the zero case.

declarations.statement_note: Line 136 omits completeness just as in the preceding identity. Lines 139–141 take the field, Lipschitz proof, L² input, and a real scalar C. The named proof hmoment states that the integral of ‖g (X ω)‖ ^ 2 is at most C. The conclusion is the L² norm bound ‖lpDrift P g hLip X‖ ≤ Real.sqrt C. C is not separately assumed nonnegative: the moment inequality and norm-square identity already imply the needed condition. The theorem converts an explicit second-moment assumption into a norm estimate; it does not establish that assumption for a stationary diffusion. The finite-measure setting and construction of the lifted drift remain the same.

declarations.name: lpUlaUpdate
declarations.title: Define one ULA update in L²
declarations.statement:
For finite \(P\), a real Hilbert space \(H\), a Lipschitz gradient \(\nabla U\), step \(h\in\mathbb R\), and \(X,Z\in L^2(P;H)\), define

\[\mathsf T_h(X,Z):=X-h\mathcal G[X]+\sqrt{2h}\,Z.\]

steps.prose: Form the drift step and add the scaled noise inside \(L^2\). All terms are already equivalence classes of square-integrable variables, so the vector-space operations produce another such class.
steps.note: Line 147. X - h • lpDrift P (gradient U) hLip X is the L² drift step using the actual lifted gradient. Spaces apply lpDrift to its measure, field, proof, and input class. The term Real.sqrt (2 * h) • Z scales the noise class by a real scalar, then + adds it to the drift step. * multiplies the real numbers 2 and h; • multiplies a scalar and an L² vector. All additions and subtractions here are operations on equivalence classes. Their representative formula must therefore be proved almost everywhere, which is the purpose of the next theorem. This line supplies data of the declared output type, rather than a proof proposition, so no by or tactic is required after the definition’s :=.

declarations.statement_note: Lines 145–146 define a single ULA step as an operation on L² classes. The potential U : H → ℝ and step h : ℝ are explicit inputs, {L : ℝ≥0} is inferred from hLip : LipschitzWith L (gradient U), and (X Z : Lp H 2 P) gives the state and noise classes. The return type is another Lp H 2 P element. := starts its defining expression. The definition itself imposes no Gaussian-law or independence condition on Z; it is a vector-space operation that can be used with any L² noise. It also permits any real h as a formal expression. Step-size and probabilistic conditions are separate hypotheses of estimates about this operation.

declarations.name: lpUlaUpdate_coe
declarations.title: The L² update is the pointwise ULA formula
declarations.statement:
For finite \(P\), a real Hilbert space \(H\), Lipschitz \(\nabla U\), and arbitrary \(X,Z\in L^2(P;H)\),

\[\mathsf T_h(X,Z)(\omega)=X(\omega)-h\nabla U(X(\omega))+\sqrt{2h}\,Z(\omega)\quad\text{a.e.}\]

This identity needs no Gaussian or independence assumption on \(Z\).

steps.prose: Expand the definition of \(\mathsf T_h\) into its subtraction, drift, and scaled-noise terms.
steps.note: Line 155. unfold lpUlaUpdate replaces the named update by the class expression X - h • lpDrift ... X + Real.sqrt (2 * h) • Z. This exposes its outer addition, subtraction, and scalar multiplications. The goal is still almost-everywhere equality with the explicit pointwise update. Expanding a definition alone does not identify arbitrary chosen representatives of these class operations; the next command supplies their almost-everywhere formulas before simplifying. See the distinction between an L² class and its representative.

steps.prose: Intersect the full-measure sets on which addition, subtraction, both scalar multiples, and the lifted gradient agree with their pointwise formulas.
steps.note:
Line 156. filter_upwards [ starts a list of almost-everywhere facts. Lp.coeFn_add gives the representative formula for the outer addition, with the drift-step class as its first argument.

Line 157. (Real.sqrt (2 * h) • Z) is the second addend. The comma ends this first premise; together these two lines give the value of the sum as the sum of representative values.

Line 158. Lp.coeFn_sub X (h • lpDrift ... X) supplies the inner subtraction formula for the drift step.

Line 159. Lp.coeFn_smul h (lpDrift ... X) handles the scalar multiplication of the lifted gradient by the step size.

Line 160. Lp.coeFn_smul (Real.sqrt (2 * h)) Z handles the scalar multiplication of the noise class.

Line 161. lpDrift_coe P (gradient U) hLip X supplies the actual-gradient formula for the drift representative. The closing ] ends the five-premise list. with ω ha hs hsm hn hg names a common outcome and the five corresponding pointwise identities. We may now reason with all these formulas at once on their common full-measure set.

steps.prose: Substitute these identities. The representative is exactly \(X(\omega)-h\nabla U(X(\omega))+\sqrt{2h}\,Z(\omega)\).
steps.note: Line 162. simp only [ha, hs, hsm, hn, hg, Pi.add_apply, Pi.sub_apply, Pi.smul_apply] substitutes the five representative formulas and evaluates pointwise function operations at ω. ha expands the outer sum, hs the inner subtraction, hsm the drift scaling, hn the noise scaling, and hg the lifted gradient. The Pi rules mean that sums, differences, and scalar multiples of functions evaluate by the corresponding operations on their values. The left side becomes exactly the pointwise expression in the statement, so simplification closes the goal. The list in simp only contains rewrite rules and local equalities, unlike the list of almost-everywhere premises in the preceding filter_upwards command.

declarations.statement_note: Lines 151–154 compare the L² update with its pointwise ULA formula. The data are the potential, real step, inferred Lipschitz constant, its gradient Lipschitz proof, and L² state/noise classes X and Z. The conclusion uses =ᵐ[P], so equality is asserted almost everywhere rather than at each outcome. On the right, the lambda returns X ω - h • gradient U (X ω) + Real.sqrt (2 * h) • Z ω. These operations take place in the original vector space H, after evaluating representatives. The formula requires no Gaussian or independence hypothesis; it identifies the algorithm’s expression, while distributional estimates can impose further assumptions separately. The proof expands the class-valued definition and combines its representative formulas.

declarations.name: lpUlaChain
declarations.title: Define the genuine L² ULA chain
declarations.statement:
For a finite measure \(P\), a Lipschitz gradient on \(E_d\), an initial class \(X_0\in L^2(P;E_d)\), and noise classes \(Z_n\in L^2(P;E_d)\), define recursively, with the supplied initial class at index zero,

\[X_{n+1}:=\mathsf T_h(X_n,Z_n).\]

steps.prose: The initial class is the supplied \(X_0\). At the successor index, apply the \(L^2\) ULA update to the preceding iterate and the next noise class \(Z_n\).
steps.note:
Line 168. | 0 => initial is the zero case of the recursive definition. The vertical bar starts a case and => separates its pattern from its value. When the final index argument is 0, the chain returns the supplied initial L² class. This is part of the definition, not a theorem to be proved by induction. The earlier parameters U, h, hLip, initial, and noise have already been fixed.

Line 169. | n + 1 => ... is the successor case, with n the preceding natural index. The body calls lpUlaUpdate P U h hLip on the preceding iterate (lpUlaChain U h hLip initial noise n) and the next supplied noise (noise n). Inside the recursive body, P is already fixed in the recursive function’s context, which explains its omission in this recursive call; external calls include the ambient explicit measure. Recursion decreases from index n + 1 to n, so Lean accepts it as terminating. The result is again an L² class because the update operation has that return type.

declarations.statement_note: Lines 165–167 define the entire noise-driven chain in the finite-dimensional state space E d. {d : ℕ} is the implicit dimension, U is the potential, h is the step, and the inferred L comes with the gradient Lipschitz proof hLip. initial : Lp (E d) 2 P is the starting class. noise : ℕ → Lp (E d) 2 P is a sequence of noise classes: noise n supplies the class at natural-number index n. The output type ℕ → Lp (E d) 2 P is likewise a sequence, not just one iterate. Instead of := followed by a single expression, Lean’s equation-style syntax gives defining cases beginning with |. They describe what the sequence returns at zero and at a successor. No distributional claim about the sequence is embedded in this definition.

declarations.name: lpUlaChain_zero
declarations.title: The initial iterate
declarations.statement: The recursively defined chain satisfies \(X_0=\mathrm{initial}\).

steps.prose: This is the zero branch of the recursion, so both sides reduce to the same class.
steps.note: Line 173. The line begins with the final parameter (noise : ℕ → Lp (E d) 2 P), then the colon introduces the equality theorem. Every argument in lpUlaChain P U h hLip initial noise 0 selects the chain data and its index. := rfl supplies the proof: rfl, short for reflexivity, allows Lean to reduce the recursive definition at index zero, where it becomes precisely initial. Thus the two sides are the same after unfolding the defining case. := introduces the proof term; the = inside the statement is the proposition proved by that term. The @[simp] attribute above means future simp calls can use this equation automatically, avoiding repeated manual unfolding of the recursive definition.

declarations.statement_note: Lines 171–173 state the zero equation for the recursive chain with the same dimension, potential, step, Lipschitz proof, starting class, and noise sequence. @[simp] is an attribute registering this proved equality as a rule for the simplifier. It is a declaration annotation, different from writing [someLemma] after a tactic. The conclusion says that evaluating lpUlaChain P U h hLip initial noise at 0 returns initial. Although the long list of parameters is repeated to make the equation generally reusable, the equation itself is exactly the zero branch of the definition. := rfl gives its proof directly, using definitional equality rather than a tactic script.

declarations.name: lpUlaChain_succ
declarations.title: The successor iterate
declarations.statement:
For every \(n\ge0\), the same finite-measure, Lipschitz-gradient, initial-class and noise-class data give

\[X_{n+1}=\mathsf T_h(X_n,Z_n).\]

steps.prose: This is the successor branch of the defining recursion; unfold that branch to obtain the equality.
steps.note: Line 179. This continuation gives the right side of the equality begun on line 178: lpUlaUpdate P U h hLip takes the preceding chain class and the class (noise n). Parentheses group each as a single argument. The final := rfl proves the equality by reducing the successor branch of lpUlaChain, after which both sides are the same expression. Reflexivity here can use definitions, so the two printed sides need not look identical before reduction. Together with the zero equation, this provides a convenient reusable rule for stepping through the recursion. The simplifier can later rewrite an occurrence at n + 1 to the update formula without expanding unrelated definitions.

declarations.statement_note: Lines 175–179 state the successor equation for the same recursively defined L² chain. As in the zero theorem, @[simp] registers the proved equation for simplification. The additional parameter (n : ℕ) is the preceding index. The left side evaluates the chain at n + 1; the right side updates its value at n using noise n. This theorem restates exactly the defining successor branch, so it requires no assumptions about Gaussian laws, independence, or a contraction factor. The proof rfl uses reduction of the recursive definition; there is no induction because we are proving one defining equation, not a property of all iterates obtained from it.

declarations.name: lpUlaChain_coe
declarations.title: Identify the chain with the original algorithm
declarations.statement:
For finite \(P\), Lipschitz gradient \(\nabla U:E_d\to E_d\), square-integrable initial and noise classes, and every \(n\ge0\),

\[X_n(\omega)=\operatorname{ulaChain}\bigl(U,h,X_0(\omega),(Z_k(\omega))_{k\ge0},n\bigr)\quad\text{for }P\text{-a.e. }\omega.\]

steps.prose: Induct on \(n\). At \(n=0\), both recursions return the same initial representative, so equality holds for every outcome. For the successor case, assume the representatives agree at index \(n\).
steps.note:
Line 188. induction n with starts natural-number induction on the index. Lean creates a zero case and a successor case, allowing the latter to assume the desired almost-everywhere equality at the preceding index. The following vertical bars label those cases.

Line 189. | zero => selects the base case. Filter.Eventually.of_forall converts an equality at every outcome into an almost-everywhere equality. The lambda fun _ ↦ rfl ignores the outcome’s name and proves the equality by reflexivity: both recursive definitions at zero reduce to the same initial representative. exact supplies this proof to close the base case. The underscore is an intentionally unused lambda input.

Line 190. | succ n ih => selects the successor case. Here n names the predecessor index and ih names the induction hypothesis, an almost-everywhere agreement of the two chains at that index. The goal is agreement at n + 1. These case-local names do not redefine the global chain.

steps.prose: On a common full-measure set, combine the one-step representative identity with the induction hypothesis. Replace \(X_n(\omega)\) by the pointwise chain’s preceding iterate and apply the two successor recursion equations. Both next iterates are the same ULA update.
steps.note:
Line 191. filter_upwards [ begins the successor case’s almost-everywhere argument. The first premise is the one-step representative theorem lpUlaUpdate_coe P U h hLip, whose state and noise arguments follow on line 192.

Line 192. (lpUlaChain P U h hLip initial noise n) and (noise n) supply that step’s current class and noise class. The second list premise is ih, so both the update formula and the previous chain agreement hold on the chosen full-measure set. with ω hupdate hprev names the outcome and the two pointwise equalities in list order.

Line 193. simpa only [...] using hupdate simplifies the existing pointwise update equality into the successor goal. lpUlaChain_succ and ulaChain_succ expose the successor equations for the lifted and original chains; ulaUpdate unfolds the pointwise update definition. The local equality hprev replaces the lifted preceding representative by the original preceding iterate. Both successor formulas then coincide, so the simplified hupdate proves the target. This completes the induction and the almost-everywhere identification of the algorithms.

declarations.statement_note: Lines 183–187 identify the lifted chain with the original pointwise algorithm at a fixed index n : ℕ. The initial and noise data are L² classes.
